div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

Mr. James Knowles, editor of the "Nineteenth Century," has sent as a New Year's gift to Mr, Andrew Carnegie the manuscript of Mr. Gladstone's article on the "Gospel of Wealth," which appeared in that review, every word of which was written by Mr. Gladstone himself.

Our able little contemporary "Woman," describes Postmaster-General Raikes as "one of the most tyrannical and despotic employers of labour in the kingdom"; and says, further, "There is no public department so steeped in jobbery and injustice as the General Pest Office."

The Emperor William is said to have sent Prince Bismarck at Christmas several photographs of the Emperor's rooms in the old Emperor William's palace. Prince Bismarck's letter of thanks was followedby a telegraphic expression of New Year's wishes hem the Emperor.

In consequence of the translation of the Bishop of Peterborough to the Archbishopric of York, the Bishop of Wakefield will be entitled to take hi& seat in the House of Lords shortly after the meeting of Parliament. The next vacancy in the Episcopal Bench will be filled by the Bishop of Chester.

The International Arbitration and :Peace Associa- tion is in particplarly good spirits. It has just received a special donation of £lO from the Marquis of Bristol, accompanied by a letter in which his lordship says: "I am sure there is a continual in- crease of the appreciation by the public of the work of the association."

1k King Kalakaua, of Hawaii, a most intelligent native monarch, who tried to keep in touch with civilisation, died on Tuesday. He died at San Francisco, and the cause of his death seems to have been the hospitality of the Ametieans. He had attended too many banquets. He suffered a slow death from urcemic poisoning.

Mr. Geo. Bancroft, America's veteran historian, whose death was announced on Monday, was over ninety years of age. He has lived quietly in Wash- ington—with oacasional visits to the seaside—since 1874, but was always engaged in. literary work. Like our own Grand Old Man he took out-door exercise every day, and his health was remarkdbly good.

Mr. Bancroft belonged to New England. He finished his education in Germany. He was ap— pointed American Minister to England in 1846, and dying the three years which he held the position spent a good deal of his time in ranSackimg the British Museum Library for the facts about the early history of America and the revolution. When he returned to America in 1850-be devoted himself to the completion of his "History of the United States." He was appointed Minister to Prussia in 11867. •
It is not good news for the public, but it may be or the Volunteers, that this branch of ,the service,

it is reported, shows a.serious falling off in numbers as compared with last year. If this should prove to be the case wheu the official return is published. it is probable that the Secretary for War will at last be forced to make those grants to the Volunteers which have been asked in vain in recent years, and thus out of evil good may come.

The Hon. and Rev. Henry Hugh Courtenay, who succeeds his nephew, the notoriously extravagant Lord Courtenay, as fourteenth Earl of Devon, is in his eightieth year. The new Earl is Rector of Mam- head and Powderham, and is also Rural Dean. Like his brother, Canon Courtenay, the Rector of Bovey Traf...3, he is n High Churchman' and during his long residence in South Devou he has earned the esteem and affection of many besides his immediate parish- ioners.

One of the most celebrated restaurateurs in Ger- many has just passed through the Bankruptcy Court, and it was discovered that among the credi- tors was a knacker, to whom nearly a thousand pounds was owing for carcasses of horses and asses. The debtor was sharply interrogated repecting this item, and he ultimately confessed that his cus- tomers had unconsciously devoured all the thousands of carcases, being there and then under the delusion that they were eating venison.

A writer in a country paper points out that in an age of "strong men," Sandows. Sampsons, and the like, the claims of the Czar of Thissia should not be overlooked. His Russian Majesty is known to be possessed of immense physical strength, and can even, it is said, tear up a whole pack ot cards if he loses his temper at halfpenny nap. Should the Nihilists ever succeed in driving Alexander 111. from his dominions. an honest living may yet be open to him by doing a" turn" at the London music-halls.

An amusing incident occurred on Tuesday night at the contert in aid of the Scottish railway men. A young and beautiful lady cast a bouquet at the feet of an artiste who sang "My Queen." He failed 'to notice this tribute, and did not pick it up, He was followed by a wild-looking Italian musician, who executed a tremendous fantasia on the violin. Well satisfied with himself he was about to descend from the platform, when he saw the bouquet almost at his feet. He smiled as though merit was at, length recognised, and, with one hand on his heart, gallantly raised the floral emblem to his lips. The audience laughed; but why he could not under- stand.

More evidence is forthcoming of the significance of the movement for raising the standard of exemp- tion fixed by various School Boards and school attendance committees. The Hon. Lyulph Stanley will, I hear, ask the liondon School Board to raise the standard in London from the sixth to the seventh. At Bristol, Mr. Walker is to , ask the School Board to raise the standard from the fifth to the sixth—a course which, I believe, is also favoured by the majority of tbe Nottingham School Board. The action of Mr. Walker has an added importance from the fact that as president of the National Union of Teachers he may be said to repre- sent the opinion of that body against the too early withdrawal of children from school.

A novelty is now to be seen on the Lake of St. Moritz. The lake is frozen over, and navigation would seem an impossibility; but an enterprising hotel-keeper has launched for his clients a new kind of yacht. It has masts and sails, and rudder and compass, though neither keel nor centre board. Its "lines" are not quite what would suit the designer of the Cunarders - in fact, in shape it is like an enormous candle-box, and the tiller and the com- pass are probably concessions to 'prejudice. But, lying on that smooth surface of ice, as hard as a mirror, and quite as polished, if the _wijid sets in the shoulder of the sail motion is easy, and a good speed soon got. They speak of twenty-five knots an hour, which would beat the Teutonic or the City of Paris.

Accounts of the locust plague in Australia are still most dismal, excepting at Adelaide, where the locusts, as was renorted just before the mails left, had been good enough to drown themselves in myriads. The seashore at Adelaide was lined with the drowned locusts. At Minyip, however, the arrival of an immense column from the north was seriously alarming the inhabitants. The atmos- phere presented the appearance of a snowstorm; the roads and fences were covered to a depth of 3in. or 4in. with a solid mass of locusts. The gardens were quickly denuded of vegetation, and all herbage was fast disappearing before the pest. The cater- pillar plague is also causing the Australian colonists serious anxiety. Failures among agriculturists are attributed to these pests ; and no wonder, when as much as £6OO is said to be the loss of one farmer alone through the destruction of his barley crop by the caterpillar.

The traditional wild beast who rushes at Royal princes in the jungle only to discover what divinity doth hedge a prince, has already made his appear- ance in the path of the Czarewitch in India. Ac- cording to the local papers, the grand sport is one of the things forbidden during the tour; but either the prince or the majestic panther that he encoun- tered in the forest near the famous caves of Ellora had apparently not beard .of this. The furious ani- mal, • disturbed in his native solitude, charged straight down upon the heir to the Imperial throne. of Russia; but luckily, or perhaps we should rather say inevitably, Prince Obolensky raised his rifle and rolled him over. The panther, however, got on his feet again, and made another rush ; but this time the merring aim of Prince pariatinsky sent thtimely ball through his brain. The creature, whose glory it has been to be thus-despatched by . two princes, is stated to measure seven and a half feet from tip to tail.

DEATH OF THE EARL OF CAITHNESS.

Information was received in Aberdeen, on Tuesday, of the death in London of the Earl of Caithness. The deceased nobleman, James Augustus Sinclair, was formerly a banker in Aberdeen, and succeeded to the title in 1889.
MURDER OF A WEALTHY GAMBLER.
TERRIBLE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A WIFE.

?.iEW YORK', MONDAY.—A negro has been arrested at Lincoln, Nebraska, on a okarge of having murdered John Sheedy, a well-known wealthy gambler. The negro confessed that he was hired by Mrs. Sheedy to murder her husband, and waste receive 20,000 dols. for doing so. The woman had obtained a divorce from her first husband, and afterwards married Sheedy, who was , many years older than herself. She recently became infatuated with a young man, whom she wished to marry, and therefore enlisted the negro's services. Last Monday night, whilst Shaedy was returning from the opera, the negro struck him on the head with a loaded cane, crushing in his skull. In his flight the murderer dropped his weapon, which proved a valuable clue to the detectives. Sheedy leaves property altogether valued at 3,400,000 dols. Five previous attempts on his life had been made.

div.head: SOCIAL QUESTION.
div.p: THE SOCIAL QUESTION.

It is a wholesome sign of the times when a great leader of religious thought and action has the cour- age to speak as Cardinal Manning does in a letter addressed by him to one of the contributors to a periodical recently published in Paris called " Le Vingtieme Siècle,' which is intended as "a review of social Christian economy." The learned Cardinal says :—" We aite strangled by exaggerated individu- alism, and next century will show that human society is greater and more noble than all that is individual. The doctrine ttat has its foundation in the law of nature and in Christianity is denounced as Socialism by the rash and the frivolous, as well as by the capitalist and the wealthy, but the future will bring into the light of reason the social status of the world of labour. We shall then discern the laws on which rests the Christian Society of man- kind. Therefore, it is a julicious work on your part to have gathered young and vigorous minds in a centre of study and publicity respecting these vital .truths. The politicians andpolitical economists of the modern school have had their day. The twentieth century will be wholly that of the people and of the laWs of the eotramon prosperity of a Christian regime."

div.head: BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.
div.p: BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.

CIIAPTER XIV. THE MYSTIC TRIBUNAL. • Away back of the old cathedral of Moscow, and in a narrow, dark court which was overlooked by the towers of the giant edifice, stood a curiously constructed stone building, which, though not con- nected bodily with the cathedral, yet seemed to be- long to it. It was low and broad, with a flat, tiled roof, and without a visible window. Within one of the apartments of this building—an apartment away down in the bowels of the earth, where the light of day never came—were seated six men. The room was of fair size, and the floor, the walls, and the ceiling were of dark stone. Wooden benches were arranged about the place; and there were some other articles of furniture there too—strange contrivances th9y were, and fashioned after various shapes and patterns. But of that anon. The place was lighted by a large hanging lamp, which had just power enough to make the room gloomy and dismal. The six men sat about a table, on which were a book and sword; and the most prominent man there was Valdimir the Monk!

And Valdimir alone exposed Hs face. All the rest wore black masks, their robes being of the same melancholy hue. They sat there silent as death, Valdimir gazing down upon the table, and the other five gazing fixedly upon him. They were stout men all of them, and they bore themselves to- wards Valdimir as bears a servant to his acknow- ledged master.

'The hour is waxing late," said Valdimir, at length looking up from the table. Ms voice sounded in that place like the echo of a tomb. It was low and hollow, and the others started as they heard it. "There's time yet to spare, master," replied one who sat next the monk. "I trust we shall not be disappointed," saidl Valdimir, at the expiration of a few moments more. To this no answer was returned. At length there came a dull echo from overhead, and the six dark sitters started up to listen. The sound grew louder, and soon it sent down into that dismal chamber the notes of coming footsteps. In a few moments more the heavy iron door creaked upon its hinges, and three men entered, and soon behind them came three more, Those who came in advance were two of them leading the third as a prisoner. And so it was with those behind. The iron door creaked again, and when the heavy bolts had been shoved into their sockets, the two pri- soners wore led forward.
"Master," spoke one of the new-comers, " we have brought the prisoners—two of them—as you commanded."
"It is well," said Valdimir. "Let them be brought before us ! "

As the two men are brought where the light can strike upon their faces we see the two guides who conducted Ruric Nevel to his place of confinement. One of them was he who met Ruric in the street, and the other is the one who guided him into the old bath-house with the lantern in his hand. They shuddered fearfully as they gazed around upon the dismal scene, and their looks plainly showed that they knew not why they had been brought thither. "Lesko Totma!" pronounced Valdimir. The first of the prisoners—he who had met Ruric in the street --started as he beard that name, and tried to speak. "Are you the man ? " asked the monk, looking into his face. "Yes, holy father," the wretch tremblingly re- plied. "Then stand you here in front of me." The fellow was moved up in front of the table, and surprise and fear seemed to be struggling for the mastery over him, for he recognized now the strange monk about whom he had probably heard so much. "Lesko Tonna," said Valdimir, lowly and slowly, "you have been seen much in the company of a humpbacked priest named Savotano. You know such a priest, do you not?" The man hesitated. He gazed furtively about him, and trembled more than before. • "Answer me! " "Yes, sir, I know him." "And now, sir, be sure that you answer ms directly and truly. Do you know a young gun- maker, named Rune Nevel ?" The fellow started with a perceptible quake as this question was asked, but he seemed to have been prepared for it, for his answer was direct. " No, sir: I do not." " Ha—beware ! Think well before you speak." "If you mean the man who fought the duel with the Count Damonoff, then I have heard of him; but I do not know that I ever saw him." "Then you are sure of this ?" " Of course I am." "Frederic Viska!" The second prisoner now came forward. He was a few years younger than his companion, though somewhat larger, and evidently more bold. Totma was conducted out of the apartment as Yiska came forward. " You, too, have been in the company of this priest, Savotano, have you not ?" The monk asked. "I know him," the fellow replied with a slight touch of defiance in his tone. He had not surely looked about him. to see those strange contrivances by which he was surrounded, or he would not ha ye ventured such a tore. ,• "And you have been some in his company? " Perhaps so." "Very Well. And now do you not also know Rune Nevel ?" "I have seen him, too, sir." "And now—can you tell me where he is at this present time ?" "No," was the answer, short and quick. "Beware ! If you have any regard for your own welfare you will answer me truly. Where is Ruric Navel ?' "I tell you I know nothing about him—nothing at all." "And of this you are sure ?" "Who are you that assume to question me thus? I know you not." Vista spoke this in a tone of virtuous indignation probably thinking that the turn might serve him. " We will let you into the secret by and by," the monk returned, with a peculiar shake of the head. " But I will ask once more: Do you know where Novel is ?" "No !" "You need not speak quite so loud. We hear easily." "Then don't ask me impertinent questions," re- torted. the prisoner. Valditnir started half-way up, and his fists were clenched ; but the quick flush passed from his face, and he sat back again. "Look ye," he said, as soon as he was sure his anger would not manifest itself, " Were I not sure that you know what I ask I would not question you thus. And now, once more. I ask you! Will you give me some clue to the whereabouts .f Rune Novel ?" "I'll answer you once more. I know nothing about him. You must not think that this dark place and you men all dressed in black, can fright me into telling a lie as it might a child." At this point Valdimir turned to one of his men —one of those who helped to bring the prisoners in —and said: "You know this to be the man ? " "Yes, my master." "And you have seen him in private confab with the humpbacked priest? " "I have." " And the other things you told me are true ? " "They are, master." " Then let down those interpreters." At this command two of the attendants moved to the back side of the room, where they unhooked a stout chain from the wall, and as they allowed it to slide through their hands a curious piece of machin- ery descended directly in front of the table. It consisted of a stout bar of iron, which was sus- pended midway, upon the chain, and there rested parallel with the ceiling. Upon each end of this bar were straps of iron, armed with springs and screws. At a motion from the monk the ptisoner was led back till he stood directly beneath the bar,and then his arms were seized and raised up. He struggled some and cursed more, but he was soon overcome. The iron bands were passed around his wrists, and esnnected with these were two small cups which were slipped over the thumbs. After these had been firmly secured the chain was tightened, and the fel- low's hands were raised far above his head. There were two results produced by tightening the chain: It not only tended to draw the thumbs back upon the wrists but it also twisted the thumb, the two cups being armed with file-like teeth within, and , closing tightly upon the flesh. .

div.head: HUNDRED AND FORTY RELIGIONS,
div.p: A HUNDRED AND FORTY RELIGIONS,

The census announcement that there are 140 re- ligious bodies in the United States, exclusive of many independent congregations, will be received with some surprise by most people whose know- ledge of different sects does not embrace more than a dozen or 20 at the most. In the list as disclosed by the preliminary bulletin issued by the Census - Bureau from Washington are the General-Six-Prin- cipal Baptists, the Schwerkfeldians, the Theosophi- cal Society, the Life and Advent Union, and others, which to a majority of the people will be entirely new. With 140 creeds formally adopted and many independent organisations with their own notimis besides, the task of those who favour Church union is difficult indeed. If only the more numerous de- nominations existed the labour of effecting a unity of Churches with regard to polity and the more essential doctrines might be easier, but what shall be said when 100 little.denominations, sturdy in their beliefs and customs, are in the field, loth to give them up?

div.head: SEVERE WEA.TIIER.
div.p: THE SEVERE WEA.TIIER.
LANDSLIP AND THREE LIVES LOST

A shocking accident befell a family in humble circum- stances, early on Wednesday morning, at Newington, two miles north of Sandgate, as the result of the lengthened frost and the sudden thaw. Between twelve and one o'clock the south-west wind blew a hurricane, and about one o'clock some hundreds of tons of earth fell from a hill, at the foot of which was an old cottage of (one floor' built of brick and plaster, the roof being thatched. In this house a whole family of six' were in their beds, and the landslip swept cottage and occupants across.the main road into a field, some 30 yard g below. The police, with other assistants, proceeded to the spot, and, after digging for a considerable time, discovered three of the inmates dead—namely, the husband, wife, and a child aged four months. All were very much crushed.

div.head: FLOODS NEAR FAVERSHAM.
div.p: FLOODS NEAR FAVERSHAM.

Shortly after 12 o'clock on TueSday, a flood occurred at Ospringo, near Favprsham,the water pouring into the houses, the inmates of which had to flee for safety with- out having time to dress or carry off any property. The men who removed the women and children, carrying them on their shoulders, had to wade through the icy water up to their armpits, while pieces of furniture, food, and other property floated in every direction. A woman Who was ill was reported missing. The flood appears to have arisen from the thaw and heavy rain on the neighbouring hills. A high rod running along the valley has been washed up for more than a mile of Its length, and in the village of Ospringe the thorough- fares are in a similar condition. One small bridge has been carried away. TWO YOUNG LADIES DROWNED.

A party of ladies and gentlemen were skating on the river Medway, near Maidstone,on Wednesday afternoon, when the ice gave way, and two ladies, cousins, were drowned. The young ladies were the . daughter and the niece of Mr.Smythe, a well-known timber merchant. The daughter had a birthday party on Tuesday night, and a birthday ball had been fixed for Wednesday night.

Snow fell intermittently over North Wales on Wednes- day, covering the mountain ranges for many miles. Upwards of 3,000 sheep have perished on the hills, ow- ing to the continued severity of the weather and the re- cent worrying of dogs. At Bridgend, Glamorganshire, an aged carrier named Jenkins, fell on the ice in the street and died shortly afterwards. It is stated that, as the result of the increased death rate in London, owing to the severe weather, the supply of black horses to remove the victims has proved insufficient, and a good many funeral hearses drawn by brown horses have been seen. The heaviest fall of snow during the present winter was experienced on Wednesday in Westmorland and Dumfriesshire.

A Reuter's Faris Telezram, dated Wednesday, says "The weather here last night was extremely unpleasant. Snow, mixed with sleet, fell fast, while violent squalls were frequent. The " Figaro " demands that the churches should be open during the night, and be transferred into retuges for the homeless poor." ' A telegram from Algiers stateelhat communication with the town of Medeah is no longer possible on account of the great depth of the snow. The conveyance of mails has ceased, and provisions in the place are becoming exhausted. Several deaths caused by cold have occurred especially amongst the natives.

div.head: "SOCIAL SALVATION." SERMON BY THE REV. J. YONGE.
div.p: "SOCIAL SALVATION." SERMON BY THE REV. J. YONGE.

On Sunday the Rev. J. YOnge preached a sermon. in Wycliffe Church, Wfrrington, the subject being "Social Salvation." His text, was Isaiah lviii.. v. 6 and 7, "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens. and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and-that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? When thou seest the naked that thou cover him, and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh ?" Having observed that this remarkable chapter might have almost been written on purpose 'for the Christendom of to-day, Mr. Yonge went on to deal with some of the social needs of the day. Referring to the work of the Committee of thu House of Lords appointed to in- quire into the sweating system, he said it wasfound that sweating went on nearly everywhere, and in some branch or other of-nearly every trade. In the report prepared by the Earl of Dunraven, who was one of the Committee, there was overwhelming proof of a terrible condition of social misery affecting large multitudes of people in various centres of population. It spoke of" sweating" as a system that invariably involved excessive hours of work, insufficient remuneration' and labour pur- sued under conditions prejudicial to physical and moral health." The report had been published at a penny a copy, and should be read by all who felt the importance of social questions. Having alluded to Geneial Booth's book, and Mr. Mearns's " Bitter Cry of Outcast London," Mr. Yonge went on to say that it was not easy for them" to shape before their minds the misery of our large towns, especially in the quarters where the poor live. It was well, how- ever, that the attempt should be made. Probably there were conditions and miseries in Warrington rookeries, which, if that respectable congregation could actually, see, would cause them to shudder. Some time ago, a local paper drew attention to the Black Soots of Warrington. He did not know with, what effect. But this he knew, that, instead of wrangling about secondary questions, their Town Council would do well to purge and cleanse away whatever" Black Spots" there might be. And any men who might be fat- tening on the unhealthy tenements where the poor were forced to live should be compelled to obey and fulfil the requirements of the sanitary law. There was room for reform in Warrington, but the conditions of Liverpool, of Manchester, of London, beggared 'description. He (Mr. Yonge) believed that General Booth's appeal would effect results outside his own scheme. He had aroused Christian attention more widely than ever before to the present ,day work of social salvation. So far from the scheme absorbing all Christian benevolence in its own par- ticular treasury,lie believed it would be ultimately found that the whole work Of Christian philan- thropy had received a tremendous stimulus, which had produced effects offinventiveness, industry, and generosity such as had never hitherto been seen. Aleneral Booth had at least effected this, that now, te-day, Social questions were to the front, and the churches of every name were realising that, if mons' souls were to be saved for the next world, their physical condition in this must be ameliorated and redeemed.

1 "Now, sir," spoke Valdimir, lowly and deeply, 1 " I am going to ask these questions again, and you J will do well to ans aver them truly. Will you tell me where Runic Novel is ? " "I don't know." " Will you tell me where you saw him last ?" " I haven't seen him since he fought the duel with Damonoff." " Beware ! " "I have not." "Mark me; I have had you watched, and I know that you have seen Nevel within these three days. This I /now, so I have no hesitation in the course I am about to pursue. Once more—Where is Runic Nevel ? " The man hesitated now ; but his answer was still the same. He would not tell. Valdimir made a motion to the two men who stood by the wall, and they gave a pull upon the chain. " Oh—God!" gasped the prisoner, as the painfig twist and wrench came upon his thumbs. " Will you answer?" " How can I? How can I?" "By speaking what you know." "1 know nothing." • Another signal was made to the men at the chain, and they pulled again. Another groan from the prisoner, but no other response. Another signal—and another pull. " Mercy !" shrieked the poor wretch, quivering with pain. "Will you answer ?" "I don't know." "Then we must try again." "No, no,—oh, God, no more !" "But you must answer." I don't know." "Then you must have forgotten, and such treacherous memories need starting up." As Valdimir thus spoke he waved his hand again. "Oh ! God have mercy! Oh-o-o ! Save me! Save me !" "Save yourself." The wretch was in torment now without ceasing. Nearly the whole of his weight bore upon his wrists and thumbs, and the latter were drawn over almost to the wrist. But he would not answer. He had a deeper fear than this. He feared to break the horrid oaths by which he was bound to the scheming priest. One more pull upon the chain, and the man's feet were clear off the floor. His whole weight now bore upon his thumbs, and he groaned in the agony of torture. He bore it a few moments, but his cow- ard soul could bear no more. "Oh, God. Down! down! Let me down!' "But answer. Where is Runic Navel?" " I—l—don't—" "Hold, thou false-lyearted villian !" shouted Val- dimir, in a voice of thunder. "This is the last of this torture; but when we take you from here we put you into a state compared with which the pain you now experience is real joy! Each par- ticular limb shall be wrenched all out of shape, and your very eyes shall start out like—" " Down ! down! Oh, great God, down !" " Where is Rune Nevel " I'll tell you-111 tell if. you spare me" "Tell me first !" There was a moment more of hesitation—one single moment—and then the miserable wretch gave up. " He s in the old bath-house. "Ha ! 'Where?" "In the old bath near the river—on the Tula pass —in one of the, vaults !" "Very well. Let him down." The chain was slacked up, and Frederic Viska was once more upon his feet. He trembled yet, for there was pain in his arms. "Now carry him out," ordered Valdimir, "and bring the other one in." In a few moments more Lesko Totma was before the strange tribunal. He trembled fearfully, for he had been where he could hear his companion's groans without hearing what he said. "Lesko Totma," spoke the monk, in a low, deep tone, "we have given you time for thought, and mayhap you have your memory brightened by this time. Now, where is Ruric Novel?" " I don't know." " Ah—you still forget, eh ?" "I never knew." "A most strange forgetfulness, I must confess. Let the interpreters be adjusted !" " Oh—mercy ! Don't murder me !" But no notice was taken of his cries. The straps and conical cups were adjusted, 'and the chain drawn tight. At the first turn of the self-acting screw the fellow shrieked. It was not so much with present pain as with the fear of what was to come. The very presage of the place, so dark and dismal, had more effect upon his mind than it had upon his companion. At the second pull of the chain he groaned and begged for mercy. He had heard of this dark place, and he fancied that men who came there seldom went away alive. "hark ye, base wretch," the monk said, "If you do not tell me where the young grn-maker is I'll have you torn limb from limb! Another' pull, there !." As the wrench came again the villain fairly shouted with pain. "Oh, let me go! Let me go! I'll tell all !" "Then tell. You leave not this place alive until you have told !" "lie is—oh, God! lle is—in the old bath!' "Where?' "The duke's bath—on the Pass of Tula!" "Whereabouts there ?" "In the lowest, furthest vault. Oh, snare r" Valdimir waved his hand, and the quaking wretch was freed from his torture. "Now, conduct them botk to the dungeons, and lock them up." They must 'not run at large for the present. Let them be secure." "No, no," cried Viska, who had seen brought back. " You were to let me go if I told you." "Not free, sir," said Valdimir. "But you have no right to hold me thus. lam nearly dead with pain now where you have torn my hands in pieces. By the " "Silence, dog ! My authority here is my power. My right is my might. I have you, and I will keep you. Were Ito let you go I might not have the power to catch you again, as legal officers could. Lead them off, and then we'll turn our attention to the Duke's Bath !" _ . -
(To be contiinieci.)

div.head: TOUCHING STORY.
div.p: A TOUCHING STORY.

A year ago, says the Helsingfors Correspondent of the "Daily News," I mentioned the peculiar mode Finland has of dealing with its paupers and aged, and I am glad to be able to say that a great deal has since been done to get the inhuman practice of selling the poor creatures by auction abolished. The Government has been awakened to the fact that the practice is barbarous and entirely out of aeCord with the otherwise cultivated institutions of Fin- land. An instance of the dreadful manner in which these auctions are held may be recorded. A very old woman, sick and weary of life, almost too feeble. to exist longer, had been sold to a farmer. Her term was up last Wednesday, when she had to be resold. It was an exceedingly cold day, and a fearful snowstorm was raging. The poor old crea- ture knew that she could not live over the night, so she asked her owner if he would allow her to die in , her corner, where she would be as quiet as possible and give no trouble, and not eat anything. She begged hard, but her request was not granted, and she was sent out to the auction. The price paid for her was very low, poor thing, for every one knew that she could not last long. After the sale was over, and the buyers were preparing to take home their purchases, the old woman was found dead. She bad kept her word. She had been no trouble to any one, but had died without a murmur.

div.head: TIT-BITS.
div.p: TIT-BITS.
ME VENTRILOQITIST.

A circutn4ance, which powerfully excited the risible muscles of a number of the town's-people, once occurred in Grimsby. It happened that Mr. Love, the ventriloquist, had publicly announced his intention of performing in the Assembly Rooms. On the appouated evening, a tolerably numerous audience had assembled; but the performance had scarcely commenced, when it was suddenly inte* rupted by the most dismal yells and howlings from above. It appears that in that part of the enter- tainment, when, by means of his singular powers of vocal deception, he causes an invisible agent to be heard singing on the roof of a building inany yards distant fsom that in which he exhibits, then gradually approaching, until it is finally heard 1 in the act of descending the chimney attached to the Assembly Moms. A native of an adjoining village, who had been induced to patronise the entertainment, and who, we presume, had never before witnessed a similar pee- formance, and consequently was not aware of the extent of the 111u3i0n which an accomplished ven- triloquist is capable of creating, felt convinced that a second person " had a finger in the p" and being well acquainted with the house, slipped out, unper- ceived by the audience, and ascended by the back stairs in the dark to the roof of the building, with the firm determination of opening the eyes of the audi- ence, and exposing the confederate of the perfprmer. At this juncture two other wiseacres in the com- pany entertained exactly the same opinion, and, accordingly, followed the steps of him who had first made his exit from the apartment. Arrived at the summit of the garret stairs, they found the tre.p-door wide open—this they thought looked suspicious, but, on ascending to the tiles they discovered the first-mentioned Paul Pry in the act of reconnoitring, with his head placed close to the chimney pot. Doubt was now out of the question; they therefore commenced belabouring their unsus- pecting victim with such vigour, that, had not his wailings brought mine host (who now began to suspect the devil was in the place in reality), and some of the people connected with the establish- ment, with lights, to his assistance, the consequence might perhaps have been rather serious. As it was, a mutual explanation speedily followed; and the ventriloquist, as might be expected, joined heartily in the covulsive roar of laughter which it occasioned, whilst the unlucky wights against whom it was directed were glad to make a precipitate retreat..

div.head: rAuLIIMENTARY SIMILES
div.p: rAuLIIMENTARY SIMILES

In one of the debates in the House of Comm Ons towards the end of the American War, Mr. Fox, in reprobating the conduct of Lord Sandwich for neglecting to expedite the building of the ships of war, spoke of him allowing the ships "to rot in their cradles." Sir George Saville, the leading country member In opposition to Lord North's ministry, in a debate on the 14th Decemer, 17i31, speaking of the address which is always understood to be a kind echo to the King's speech, observed—" This echo had always been, and this echo would perpetually continue, and in so ridiculous a degree, that were the speech trom the throne a repetition of the line— What beauties does Flora disclose!'

the echo from that house would fill up the couplet, and reply, 'How sweet are lin smiles upon Tweed r In fact, the crown and the two houses danced a minuet together to a tune of the minister's compo- sing. The crown led off one way; the two houses, in a similar step to the opposite corner; then they joined hands, and at length finished just as the dance began." In a debate on the 22nd February, 1782, Mr. Burke, speaking of Mr. Welbore Ellis, who, from the c njoyment of a lucrative sinecure, had been called to the active appointment of American secretary, as successor to Lord George Germaine, remarked, that n "being of the caterpillar species, he had remained within the soft and silken folds of an extremely valuable employment, till, having burst his liga- ments, he fluttered forth the minister of the day. • an insect as to exter!ors transformed, but inwardl3 and at heart the same."
PROGNOSTICS DRAWN FROM TERRESTRIAI
BODIES.

1. If the flame of the lamp sparkles, or if it forms an excrescence, there will be, in that case, a strong probability of rain. 2. The same happens when the soot loosens and falls down the chimneys. 3. If the coals in the grate blaze more than usual, or name with more activity, it is a sign of wind. 4. On the-contrary, when the flame is steady and uniform, it is a s:gn of fair weather; when the flame is low and blue, it is a certain indication of frost. 6. If the sound of bells is heard from afar, it is a sign of wind, or a change of weather. 6. If pleasant or offensive smells are condensed, that is, become stronger, they indicate rain. 7. The frequent change of wind is the forerunner of a violent storm. 8. If salt, marble, iron, or glass, become moist— if the wood of doors and windows smells, and becomes distended—and if the corns on the feet become painful, these are symptoms of rain or a thaw.

9. Those winds that begin to blow in the day time, are always more violent, and ktst longer, than those that begin during the night. 10. The frost that begins with wind lasts longest. 11. If the wind does not change, the weather seldom changes. 12. If distant objects become more than usually distinct, and appear nearer than usual, it is a csp. tam n precursor of rain.

PROGNOSTICS OF THE WEATHER DBAwri FROM ANIMALS. The following have, from long observation by several meteorologists, been found to afford pretty certain indications of atmospherical changes :- 1. When the bats appear more numerous than ordinary, and ily abroad longer than usual, they announce fine and warm weather on the following day. The contrary is the case when they are fewer than usual, and when they take refuge in houses and cry. 2. The owl, when it is heard crying in bad weather. is the forerunner of fine weather. 3. The croaking of ravens in the morning indicate* the same. 4. It is a symptom of approaching rain and storms. when ducks and geese fly here and there in fine weather, and dive into the water. 5. When the bees make short excursions fro?* their hives, it is a symptom of rain; aud it is equally so when they come in swarms to the hive before night end without being completely laden. 6. If the pigeons return late to the pigeon-house. they announce rain for the following day. 7. It is a sign of bad weather, when the sparrowes chirp frequently, and invite each other to flock together. 8. When the hens roll themselves in the dust more than usual, it is a symptom of coming rain ; and it is an indication of the same when the cocks crow in the night at extraordinary hours. 9. It is a sign of bad weather when the swallnvre skim the surface of the water or the ground; and when they hawk very high in the atmosphere, it is a sure indication of continued droeght. 10. A storm is approaching when the flies sting and become more troublesome than usual. 11.. When the gnats assemble before Emmet, and form a circling mass, they announce fine weather. la. If the frogs croak more than nsual„ and te the toads come out in great numbers from their holes in the evening—if the worms appear on the sarlace of the soil--if the moles labour more thse usual—and if the oxen and the turkeys collect to- gether, these prognosticate almost evident certainti of rain. 13. When the catt/e in the fields, especially tl3! sheep, are sharper than usual after the grass, rain ha' not far distant. 14. When cats lick their paws frequentbe rub threni over their faces, it is a sure indication ob raiz. 15. When cattle congregate, and remain in ell masses, in an inactive state, it is an indicatiOn the approach of thunder.

EIOUSE OF LORDS, TrarIZSDAY.

Their lordships reassembled after the Christmas recess. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past fourlitlock, and there were about forty peers in attendance. Coonsu (or BUSINFSS.—Eart (RANVILLE • asked the Prime Minister what was likely to be the course of busi- ness in their lordships' house. —The Marquis of SALMI:TRY said there were two important bills—the Tithes Bill and the bill affecting Scotch private business—whieh were in an advanced stage before the other house, and were likelytto come before their isrdships before very long. As to any further business, he would rather waitto see what bills were submitted before making any suggestion. INSURANCE OF CEIVORES.—The Bishop of reterborough '(Archbishop-designateof York), moved the second read- ing of the Children's Life Assurance Bill, and was greeted 'with cheers. lie reminded their lordships that last year they gave a second retding to the measure, and referred dt to a select committee, whose labours had not been com- pleted when the session came to an end. The Bill was read a second time, ,and ordered to be referred to a Select 'Committee. . . _
Their lordships •-adjourned at ti minutes to five o'clock.
HOUSE KIF COMMONS.—Tsurt.stm.y.

The Speaker took the chair at a:Tee o'clock. A large attendance of members was present. This morning, the first occasion .en which the Speaker has occupied the chair during *represent session, all the members present went through 'the customary ceremony of handshaking With him. I.lr. Parnell entered the House shortly after prayers. NOTICE 011" MOTION.—The following notices of motion were given;:—Mr. Stansfeld to call attention to the Parlia- mentary Franchise and move a resolution. Mr. Parnell to call attention to the administration of the Crimes Act in Irelandend move a resolution, and to-morrow evening to ask the 'First Lord of the Treasury whether he will give facilities for the discussion of the motion. NEW MtllßEE.—Sir Jolrn Pope Hennessy, who was introduced by Mr. Justin M'Carthy and Mr. Sexton., took his.seat for North Kilkenny, in the room ot the late Mr. Marum. The hon. member was greeted with lend Oppostken and ditti-rarnellite cheers.

-tHE SUICIDE OF TILE DUKE OF BEDFORD.—Mr. CORR asked the Hdme Secretary whether it was true, asstated in thelLondon press, that a coroner's inquiry was held into the circumstances attending the death of the late Dukie,of Bedford ;whether it is the custom in these.cases to give notice to the police of the holding of such in- quir:; if it was done in this case, whether the Home Office-will obtain full information of the cause 'cif this case-being treated diffeiently from any other case and as to the secret nature of the inquiry.—Mr. MAYTTREWS asked the hon. gentleman to allow him to artswer the question to-morrowyes he had only just reached 'Lon- don. • , Tut STRIKE IN SCCTLAND.—.III reply LO a question, Sir M. 'PRIVATE BILL ?LEGISLATION. The LOTO34ITTOCATE moved the second reading of the Private Bill procedure ‘(Scotland). The subject of private bill legislation, he said, bad excited more interest in Scotland than in -any other :part of the United Kingdom, and probably the,incon- Nenience resulting from existing arrangements in this respect was more keenly felt there. Mr. C AMP- &BELL BANNERMAN moved an amendment -setting 'forth-that the subjects dealt with in private bill 'legislation ought not to be committed for 'inquiry to a 'commission until it has been shown that itis impractic- • able to remedy the evils now complained .M by amend- ing the present system of inquiry by Ffeliament, and • tkttentling the powers of municipal and local authorities. -A discussion, confined almost exclusively to -Scotch "members, followed, and the bill, after a division, ,was 'real a second time and referred to a SelecteCommittee. The House adjourned at five minutes npast 'twelve o'clock.
THE gARTLEPOOLS ELECTION.
GREAT LIBERAL TRIM,

The polling in the Hartlepool, to -fill the ‘vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Richardson, 'Dissentient 'Liberal, took place on Wednesday, and the .result was declared-shortly before mid-niht as follows!: Mr. C. Furness (L.).......... '4,603 ir W. Gray (D.L.) . 4,305

• Majority.-- 298 This; is'a gain of a seat to the Liberal party. We append 'the figures for the last two electi3ns: 1285. 'lBB6. Mr. T. Richardson (L) 3.669 11.1 r. T. Richardson (D:L.) 3.381 Dr. T. H. Tristram (C) 2,629 Mr. M. L Hawkes (L.) 2,469 Liberal Majority 1,040 D majority 912 The number of voters has increased since MlB6 by •about two thousand. But on Wednesday the votes recorded numbered 3,058 more than in 1886:; -so that, assuming that all the new voters went to the poll, more than a thousand electors who held bad& at the last election must now have made up their winds for or against Home 'Rule, and voted accordingly. The Liberal and Conservative poll respectively at the present and two Preceding.elections may be shown thus: 1885. 5886. 18E1 Liberal Conserve:l've 2,629 ... .3,381 ... 4,306 The announcement of the victory of Mr. Furness over Sir William Gray was received throughout the Hattie- pools with intense satisfaction. Middlegate-st., in front of the Borough-buildings, had been crowded for hours with anxious spectators, numbering about 6,000. 'Hoe counting-was unusually prolonged, owing to the Union- ist agents being exceptionally particultr with regard to the pipers.ainethe amount of time consumed in verify- ing the returns brought in by the returning officers. The Mayor announced the result in the midst of a severe ; snowstorm. There was an intense jubilation among the • working classes when it was known that Mr. Furness ' had been returned. He was wildly cheered on making his appearance in the streets and his progress to the rail- way station, where a special train was in waiting, was a triumphal one. On arriving at West Hartlepool there were again deaf- ening cheers, and all down Church-street to the Royal Hotel and Lynn-street, the joy of the people was ex- Pressed in a most extraordinary manner. Mr. Furness has all:along ,been confident of a victory,but the effects of Sir William Gray's supporters were so desperate that even some of those who believed in Mr. Furness's suc- cess began to waver somewhat in their forecast. Sir Wlliam Gray looked unutterably woe-begone to-night when he came down the staircase from the counting- room to the room where the result was declared. Mr. Furness, M.P. after arriving at West Hartlepool, proceeded to the Liberal Club, where he delivered a brief address, stating his belief that he had won because he was true to the principles enunciated by Mr. Gladstone, and desired to do justice to Ireland. Mr. Furness stated that previous to the counting taking place he and Sir William Gray shook hands, and mutually resolved that they should remain as staunch friends in the future as in the past, whatever the result might be. The new mem- ber, amid much merriment, pictured the sad faces in the counting-chamber of Sir H. Havelock-Allan, the Union- ist member for South-East Durham, and two prominent Tories, Dr. Gourley and Colonel Cameron. He had, before even addressing, that audience, wired to Mr. Glad- stone the result, and he had no doubyie would be glad to know the at of the Hartlepools.

- . - MR. GLADSTONE'S OPINION. The Central News says: In reply to a telegram asking his opinion upon the indications afforded by the result of Polling in the Hartlepool boroughs, Mr. Gladstone tele- graphs this afternoon :—" The Hartlepool election is, from time and circumstances, by far the most important sinee 1886. The limits of a message preclude my giving my full meaning, but all must see that the simple figures of the poll reduce to dust and ashes the declarations of Lord Salisbury, Sir Henry James, Mr. Goschen, and the Duke of Westminster on what they call recent events."

div.head: SIR HENRY JAMES AT BURY.
div.p: SIR HENRY JAMES AT BURY.

Sir Henry James addressed a somewhat divided meet- mg of his constituents at Bury on Monday night. He confessed that until reczntly there had been a fear amoug Liberal Unionists that the hour of their vindication would be delayed until Home Rule had been granted to Ireland and had produced disaster to the empire. Recent events, however, had justified their action in time. A vote of confidence in the member was carried by a majority.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT CAMBRIDGE.

The Marquis of Salisbury arrived at Cambridge en Wednesday afternoon, from Hatfield, in order to bc pre- sent at a great Conserva.tive meeting. He was received on the platform by the Mayor (Mr. F. C. Wace), Mr. 11. Penrose Fitzgerald, M.P., Sir C. Hall, M.P. Mr. J. Haugh (the leader of the Conservative party in the borough), and the Hon. and Rev. Latimer Neville, the Master of Magdalene College. He drove with Mr. Neville, his host, to the Master's Lodge at Magdalene College, where a select party were invited to meet him at dinner. The rneeting was held at eight o'clock in the Corn Exchange, a building which holds three thousand persons. Great eagernes,s was shown in the town to procure tickets for the meeting. There was a considerable number of Univer- sity fellows and professors and many ladies were pre- sent. There were also in the meeting not a few students, ho indulged in the humours peculiar to their light- earted tribe. When Lord Salisbury entered he was rteeived with every demonstration of respect. Mr. Pen- lose Fitzgerald, M.P., presided, and he was supported by Mr. Raikes, M.P. Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P. Mr. C. tall, m.p G . Pro. Sir . Stokes, M.P., Mr. Smith Barry, the Hon. H. Neville, Prof. Sidgwick, Mr. F. A. fjster, Prof. Seeley, Prof. Emery, Mr. Giffard Q.C. yonservative candidate for the Newmarket Division of I;aciribriclgeshire.)—Mr. James Hough, a leader of the o 1°,4. Primrose League, presented an address to Lord t'4l bury on behalf of several Conservative organisations In Cambridge. Lord Salisbury in responding, said the Irish members Ram provided for the country a merry Christmas. He

• tidiciled Mr. Morley's statement that the Home Rule campaign had been almost won before the recent Icvela- dens. Nor did he believe that these disclosures had killed et, A vigorous struggle .still lay before the Conservative pally. There had been a rehearsal of Home Rule in action. It seemed an evolution from Donnybrook Fair; whatever happened in Ireland ran to blackthorns. It all showed that the dominant section of the Irish were still far from the development which would fit them for the Parliamentary system.. It was wholly under priestly influence, whicheuiluence, if Home Rule werc granted, would govern Ireland for the future. Ulster could not be placed under the sinister dominion of Archbishop Croke and Archbishop Walsh. Lord Salisbury argued that though discontent took a political form it was caused really by physical misery- This was largely due to the character of the country, and partly to the habits of the pewle. The Government were seeking to im- prove the disadvantageous physical conditions by aug- menting the means of conveyance and increasing the peasant proprietary. The ownership of the soil would. he believed, promote thrift and industry, and incline the surplus population to emigration. • IRELAND.

div.head: MR. HEALY AT LONGFORD.
div.p: MR. HEALY AT LONGFORD.

_ Mr.. T. M. Healy, M.P., was among his constituents in North Longford on Sunday. He, together with Mr. Arthur O'Connor, M.P. attended a large meeting of his constituents and severely attacked Mr. Parnell, whose leadership he said he would never again acknowledge. While the meeting was being held the platform collapsed, and all upon it fell to.the ground. No one was injured, but several, including Mr. Healey, got a shaking. •

div.head: DISTRESS FUND.
div.p: THE DISTRESS FUND.

Subscriptions are stiil-Wti;ing—itit:;;Dui3lin Castle, and a large staff of officials were engaged on Saturday ar- ranging the distribution cf the fund. Numerous appii- 'cations for relief are being received. The fund now .exceeds £30,000.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AT TRALEE.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AT TRALEE.

The promised visit of Mr. Parnell to Tralee was paid on Sunday. At various places on the way front Dublin the hon. member was cheered by gatherings of his sup- porters, and at the end of his journey was very cordially 'received. Replying after the presentation of several addresses, Mr. Parnell dwelt upon the legislative advan- tages which had been secured for• Ireland under his leadership of the Irish party, and specially referred to measuresput forward for the solution of the land ques- tion. As for the present position of the Irish party, the part he was able to discharge in putting an end to their differences was done when he met Mr. O'Brien and came to an understanding with him a fortnight ago. He .knew not what had happened since. There had been great delay, but it was not of his own origin.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AT ATHLONE.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AT ATHLONE.

Mr. Parne-11;isited Athlone on Monday, and made two -speeches. Addressing a large gathering in the afternoon, he expressed the utmost confidence that he would come victorious out of the presene struggle. Further' he charged the people to have patience. With that, he felt certain that they would ultimately gat a better measure of Home Rule than if they had accepted the maimed and whittled-down scheme of Mr. Gladstone. MR. DILLON'S ARRIVAL. -

—... —.— Mr. John Dillon, M.P., was received on his arrival at Havre from New York on Sunday by Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Gill, who had travelled from, Paris expressly to meet him. The meeting beween the hon. member and his Parliamen- tary colleagues wgikof the most cordial description. In the course of a bfff conversatitm, he stated that he was unable to make any communication of the question of Irish leadership until he had an opportunity of discussing the situation at length with his colleagues. The Home Rulers then drove to their hotel, and after lunching to- gether remained in close consultation, the letters which Mr. Dilion had received furniAing apparently much matter for anxious consideration. •

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P.., who is staying with his father-in-law in Paris, on Tuesday dictated a letter to a Press representative, in which he stated that substan- tial progress had been made towards the settlement which would be satisfactory to British as well as Irish sentiment. Mr. Dillon and he would not leave France without exhausting every .effort for peace, and very few days must determine the result.

div.head: SEVERE D] ORESS IN WA RRI NGTON.
div.p: SEVERE D] ORESS IN WA RRI NGTON.

It is satisfactory to learn that an the one hand the distress existing in Warrington through the long duration of unfavourable weather, has not been so severe as it has conisnonly been supposed to be, and that, on the other hand,prompt andearnest measures are, being taken to deal with the large amount that, we are sorry to say really does exist. The Charity. Organisation Society- has this week been abun- dantly justifying its existence, so far as Warrington is concerned, by employing a number of poor women in making up articles, of clothing; and by season- able and comforting 'distributions of coal and soup. The Rector (tale Rev. F. W. Willis), ,as will be seen from our ;report of Mr. R. Davies's timely and considerate appeal to the a 3 ench on be- half of the suffering poor,was early in the field, be- stirring himself, happily with much success, in the cause of those who were so ill-provided against such an emergency as thatin which they have becn placed by the rigours 'te this exceptional winter. The Aged People's Treat Cornmittee,no doubt seeing the inadvisability of two charitable agencies acting quite independently, and perhaps thus 'overlapping each other, and to some extent, neutralising the good done, have Co-operated with the Charity Or- ganisation Society; and the public have thus the assurance that the work of relief is being carried out iii something like a methodical and a compre- hensive way. It is to be hoped that the elements will concur with the praiseworthy and philanthro- pic efforts now being put forth, and soon make the renewal of suspended industries possible. In the meantime, funds are urgently needed, and it is to be hoped that there will be a generous response to the appeal which the Mayor has made.

div.head: APPLICATION TO TILE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: APPLICATION TO TILE MAGISTRATES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Robert Davies said he had ventured to attend there that day to make an application to the Bench in consequence of the distress which pre- vailed to a great extent in the town; 4ind was caused by the excessive severity of the weather. The Board of Guardians, he knew, were somewhat cir- cumscribed by. the rules, laid dqwn for them, but the time had come xlien there really should be something done in Warrington to meet the distress which existed Amongst certain classes. He felt sure that if their worships could approach the question ' in some way, and put themselves at the head of a movement for the relief of what was really becom- ing a serious amount of distress, something would be accomplished. There. were, it was true, good wages being paid in certain trades, but there must be many men in Warrington, agricultural labourers, bricklayers' labourers, canal men, and others, and men connected with trades which he dared say he knew nothing about, who must have been unable to do any work for the last few weeks. lie understood that the Rector of Warrington had made an appeal to the charitable, and it had been responded to to some extent. In Stockton Heath enquiry had been made of the contrac- ' tor for the Ship Canal, and he had been exceed- ingly good to his man, having been advancing to them, although not sure of their appearing, money in anticipa- tion of the work they would do. Tickets had also to some extent been distributed, therefore he did not think there was very great distress there. But in Warring- ton there was a great deal. One example he might give. A man came to him on Saturday morning and said, "I have never begged before, I live with my father and mother, and if we can only get a two pound loaf and a quart of soup we can go on." He (Mr. Davies) said "Have you no fire ? "and the man replied' Oh, I don't care about fire if we can get something to eat." As one of their oldest native inhabitants of Warrington, it occurred to him,when he read that morning about Supt. Bent, and the soup kitchens, at Old Trafford, to come and make an appeal to their worships. He had a letter from one of the vicars that morning in which he was asked to help to relieve the distress, as it was more than he could cope with. He (the applicant) had heard ex- pressions of opinion in the town which induced him to think that something might be done. Of course he hoped this weather would change,but he was old enough to remember the frost of 1837, when there was very great distress, and so far as he could see from the papers the present weather was very much the same all over the continent, and he saw no sign of it break- ing up. Perhaps their worships would kindly think the matter over. He did not ask for any hasty expres- sion of opinion; but left the subject for their considera- tion. The MAYOR said it was very kind and considerate on Mr. Davies's part to take this matter up, but already he himself had enquired from every source possible, and those who had given him information had not been of opinion that the poverty had been of such a severe character asthat gentleman seemed to think. He (the Mayor) had only on Thursday, asked Mr. Hunt about the matter, he and his inspectors being in a position to know a good deal as to the state of the town; and had also made other inquiries, and found that every trade in the town with the exception of just the few Mr. Davies mentioned was exceedingly busy. He heard only yesterday that the fustian-cutting trade was so busy that sufficient hands could not be obtained for it. That of course, was an exceedingly good thing if it was true. But he would promise that he would take the matter up with his brother magistrates, and if they could possibly see their way to do anything to relieve suffering they would be only pleased to do Mr. DAVIES said he thanked his worship. What had been said was all that he could have expected. He believed his worship was perfectly right as to the par- ticular trade he had mentioned. Alderman HARRISON saki he was afraid Mr

div.head: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 24, 1891.
div.p: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 24, 1891.

Davies had not exaggerated the severity of the crisis, and he himself believed that there was a vast deal more distress beneath the surface than anyone had the slightest idea of. He vqs speaking now from hearsay, as one closely connected with one who was in the habit of going into the back slums of Warrington; and the pitiable picture he drew of what he had witnessed of the terrible sufferings endured there, was enough to make one's heart bleed. He was glad Mr. Davies had mentioned this subject, and was sure that everybody must feel with him that something should be done and must be done. It so happened that no one could set a movement on foot, with any show of authority, except the chief magistrate, as without him n.o public meeting could very well be called to consider the subject. He was sure therefore that the Mayor was the one to bring the question before the town, and that what Mr. Davies said that morning would not have been in vain. Alderman Surrox said he might just tell Mr. Davies that the distress in the town had been so forcibly re- presented to him during the last day or two that, as president of the old people's treat Committee, he had made arrangements that very morning for a meeting of the Committee at his office that night, in order to see if they could do something to allay the distress in the town. He quite agreed with Mr. Davies and Mr. Harrison that there was a great deal of distress, not so much particularly in the trades that the Mayor had named ,but in trades in which, although there might be plenty of work, the men were, on account of the frost, quite unable to do it. He had no doubt that the aged people's Christmas Treat Committee would be induced to do something. At the same time the Mayor would do very well to take this matter into considera- tion, and possibly call a meeting of the inhabitants in order to consider the question, as it was very essential that something should be done. Mr. DAVIES said he quite felt that their worships could only act on the information they had received, and that it would satisfy the public to some extent to have had this discussion. Alderman DAVIES said he had in some measure anti- cipated the distress, and had subscribed to the various clergy of the town for the relief, as far as possible, of those in want. Chief Constable HUNT said it was not until .about the- early part of last week that he had any idea there was so much poverty and distress in the town as there was now. But from what he could hear, he knew there was now a very great deal. There were not so many people in the streets, and the public- houses were not so much frequented. He had never seen poor people, as he thought, so well pro- vided with money and all the necessaries of life to overflowing as at Christmas and New Year's time. It was only within the last week or two, he thought that the shoe had begun to pinch. Alderman HARRISON said it had not begun to pinch them sooner so much, for the simple reason,that a great many of them had denuded themselves of almost every article of clothing,and the like,in order to keep body and soul together. Hence the distress might not have appeared to some people who had only taken a superficial view of it, so intense as it really had been. His wife was telling him only the other day that she west into a cottage and there was hardly anything in the place in the shape of furniture,and the poor man's shoes had been taken off his feet and carried to the pawn-shop to raise money to keep the bailiffs out of the house for rent. The poor woman had simply 'a thin dress over her body, and nothing underneath it, and she told Mrs. Harrison that the had had to take everything to the pledge in order to obtain food for herself and children. So that there was a good deal of distress which did not come to the surface. Chief Constable HUNT said there were a great many houses in the low part of Warrington which were occu- pied by strangers who had just come to the town, especi- ally canal labourers. They would get a chair and a three-legged stool and occupy a house. Alderman DAVIES: There is ample opportunity for us to give our. money. Mr. DAVIES said he was quite satisfied with the result of the discussion.because he felt sure their worships would make every enquiry. He believed it wa,s a faetthat most of the tradesmen of the town were doing well, but there was certain canal labourers' werk which was entirely stopped. The MAYOR: There are, sir. Mr. DAVIES then -thanked the magistrates. and bade them good morning.

ment in the fustian cutting trade in the town. Work at the tanneries was also in a better condition. A long dis- cussion took place, after which it was decided to render as much assistance to the poor as the state of the Com- mittee's funds would allow. An adjourned meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon, at Alderman Wright's office in Sankey-st., that gentleman being in the chair, and it was resolved to render assistance to the relief movement through the Charity Organisation. Another meeting of the Committee was held on Tuesday evening, when the Mayor and Town Clerk were among those present. It was resolved to provide soup dinners daily from twelve to two, in the Drill Hall, for poor children, and the first dinner being given en Wednesday. The Com- mittee subscribe to the cost, but an appeal is to be made to the public for assistance. The preparation of the soup has been entrusted to Mrs. Booth, who is an excellent cook, and who rendered valuable service on the occasion of the Jut season of serious distress in Warrington. No doubt many ladies will be found to give their services at the Drill Hall, the use of which has been kindly placed at the disposal of the Committee by Lieutenant-Colonel Bolton and other officers. At the conclusion of the meeting, several mem- bers of the Committee paid a visit to the rooms of the Charity Organisation Society, and expressed their plea- surable astonishment to find that such a good work was being done, and on such an extensive scale. Among the applicants for admission to the room was a destitute woman who begged to be admitted, even if no remun- eration was given to her, expressing her readiness to give her services in seturn for the privilege of sitting near the fire. The poor creature, it is unnecessary to say, was allowed the boon she so touchingly appealed for ; and the incident in itself constitutes perhaps a more eloquent illustration of the misery that poverty is creating in certain quarters of the towp at present, than anything that we could write.

div.head: CHARITY ORGANISATION SOCIETY'S PROVISION.
div.p: THE CHARITY ORGANISATION SOCIETY'S PROVISION.

On Tuesday a large number of poor women were em- ployed in sewing at the King-st. rooms, and in addition to their usual refreshments, in some of the most urgent cases, their families were supplied with good wholesome soup and bread. During the afternoon several gentle- men waited on Mrs. Harrison. at the King-st. rooms, and after what they saw and heard, resolved to take steps forthwith to extend the relief to many poor families who were grievously suffering through the extreme severity of the weather, and, we understand, that it was resolved at a meeting held on Tuesday night to give free dinners to poor children each day for at least a Nteek at the Drill Hall.

div.head: AGED PEOPLE'S 'TREAT COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE AGED PEOPLE'S 'TREAT COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Old Men's Dinner and Aged Women's Tea Committee was held on Monday evening, at the offices of the President (Alderman Sutton), Legh-st., for the consideration of the steps to be taken by the Com- mittee alleviating the distress in the borough. In the absence of the President, Alderman Wright (hon. sec.), ,presided, and the other members present were—Messrs. 'Charles Skinner, George Pilling, James Smethurst, Peter Chrimes, Samuel Jones, and ID. Fanshaw. It was reported that there was a balance in the bank in favour of the Committee; and one of the members remarked that it was pleasing to know that there had been an improve-

div.head: SKITING ON NEWTON LAKE.
div.p: SKITING ON NEWTON LAKE.

, It is now something like ten years since skating has been indulged in on Newton Lake, to the ex- tent which has recently prevailed. For a week or so skating has more or less been the rule on the very large sheet of ice which covers the waters of the lake. No sooner does the fact become known that the ice is in splendid condition,than crowds of people flock from all the outlying villages to the lake, and eon the surface is studded with some hundreds of skaters gliding about from end, to end of the ice. On Saturday a great many people thronged the ice, which was in prime condition, but on Sunday, the number of those on the ice might be reckoned by the thousand. All sorts and conditions of men and women were present,and the scenes to be witnessed were hardly in keeping with the day. Hot potatoes were being briskly sold, and the purveyor, it is said, did a roaring business. Several matches for small sums of money were decided, but the event of the day was the appearance of a man on skates,clad in the very scantiest of attire; in fact, he was dressed for a bath in the waters of the lake, if such a contingency became necessary. The police, how- ever, got wind of this outrage on decency, and the man, who was training for a match, together with his supporters, beat a hasty retreat. A beautiful moonlight night•followed, and many people re- mained on the ice until a late hour. On Monday one or two matches were brought off, but the slight fill of snow had, to a certain extent, spoiled the previous glass-like surface.

div.head: KITCHEN BOILER EXPLOSIONS.
div.p: KITCHEN BOILER EXPLOSIONS.
A WOMAN KILLED,

On Monday afternoon a kitchen boiler explosion took place at the house of Mr. Grannell, bookkeeper, Lothier-, road, Anfield, near Liverpool. The water supply pipes were frozen, and though Mrs. Grannell was advised by her husband and a neighbour to put out the fire she did not do so. The kitchen and its furniture were wrecked, and when discovered Mrs. Grannell was lying in a cor- ner with her forehead fearfully injured and her body scalded. She died before medical aid 'arrived. At noon on Monday, a kitchen boiler explosion, attri- butable to the severe frost, took place at Hanley, when the house of Mr.Cornes, a builder, was wrecked, and his two daughters aged fifteen and ben injured, one of them not being expected to recover.

div.head: TWO CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH.
div.p: TWO CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH.
A JURYMAN FINED,

On Monday morning, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lancashire, held an inquest at the Railway Hotel, St. Helens Junction, on the body of Thomas Ralph Evans, two years of age, son of Aaron Evans, collier, 4, Powder Works-yard, Sutton, who was fatally burned on Friday. The inquest was delayed for a few minutes by the absence of a juror, and Police- constable Rigby stated that he warned Alfred Hardy, a publican, residing in Norman's-lane, to attend as a juror. Hardy told him that he shonld not do so, and he (Police-constable Rigby) replied that he would have to comply with the warning. Hardy again replied, "I shan't come."—The Coroner said he did not think jurors ought to say that. It was an unpleasant duty they had , to perform. As citizens everyone had to perform duties, some of which were paid for and some of which were not. He himself had to perform many duties for which he received no remuneration, and he did them as willingly as those for which he received payment. Under the new Coroners' Act a jury- man was liable to a penalty Of £5 if he • did not attend when warned, and he would fine Hardy 40s. p The police could also inform him that there was no necessity to communicate with him (the coroner) and ask him to remit the fine, because he should not do so. He, therefore, need not trouble him with any letters so long as he wilfully disobeyed the orders of the court. , He called for another juror, and Constable Rigby officiated.—Evidence was then given to the effect that on i Friday Mrs. Evans was called to a neighbour's house. , The boy was sitting on a stool near the fire, and two other children were in the house. A cinder fell from the , grate and ignited the boy's night-dress. A lad named Grice ran into the house, and severely burned his_hand in attempting to put out the flames. The deceased was badly burned about the body, and expired a few hours later.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and the boy Grice was complimented for his bravery, one of the jurors handing him a substantial sum of money. On Monday afternoon Elleti Hodkisson, two years of age, daughter of Ralph Hruclkisson, collier, of 3, Back- lane, St. Helens, died from burns received on Sunday afternoon. The deceased was left in the house alone while the mother visited a neighbour's •'house. During her absence the child's clothes got ignited by some means, and before the flames were extinguished severe injuries were inflicted. Dr. Herbert Knowles was called, and attended the child up to her death. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall, on Thursday, concerning the death.— The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental, death."

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A ST. HELENS GENTLEMAN.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A ST. HELENS GENTLEMAN.

At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, be fore Colonel F. W. Earle and Alderman J.C. Gamblejohn Charles Harvey. of Eccleston Hall, near St. Helens, was summoned by the Inland Revenue authorities for killing game. without a license, on the 14th October last. Mr. Heald, district supervisor of In- land Revenue, prosecuted, and Mr. H. L. Riley de- fended. Mr. Heald stated that on the date named Joseph Frankland, a gamekeeper, secreted himself near Mr. Harvey's house, and after waiting for some time he saw Mr. Harvey come out of the front door of the hall with a gun in his hand. Mr. Harvey pointed the gun towards some shrubs in his garden, and fired twice. He then went towards the spot where he had fired, and the game- keeper saw him return with a pheasant in one hand and his gun in the other. The gamekeeper got on the railings and whistled, and Mr. Harvey turned round, and on see- ing the keeper he ran into the house with the gun and the pheasant. The gamekeeper then went into the grounds where he thought the game had come from, and he there saw some pheasant's feathers atid a few leaves with the marks of shot upon them. He (Mr. Heald) understood the defence would'be an alibi, but Mr. Stub- ley, a corn miller, of Eccleston, would prove that be- tween ten and eleven o'clock on the day in question, he was passing Mr. Harvey's house, and saw Mr. Harvey in the garden.—Joseph Frankland, gamekeeper, Joseph Stubley, corn miller, Eccleston, and Abel Latham, a joiner at Eccleston Lodge, then gave evidence.—Mr. Riley, for the defence, said that hecould not disguise the fact that the issue of the case was one ef perjury, and it was for the Bench to say on which side the truth lay. Mr. Harvey's mouth was closed by Act of Parliament, but he solemnly declared through him (Mr. Riley) that Frankland's story was a wicked fabrication; that he never shot a gun, that he never went out of his house by the front door, and that at the time alleged he was either on his way to Liverpool or was in Liverpool.— John Rich, gardener in the employ of Mr. Harvey, Mrs. Rich, and Mr. John Henry Townley, auctioneer and valuer, 129, Dale-st., Liverpool, were called as witnesses. —After a hearing of some hours, the Bench retired,- and on their return the Chairman said they had given the case every attention. Although they thought there were certain points of the evidence strong against the defen- dent, they had their doubts in the case, and they there- fore dismissed the information.
