REPORT OF TILE INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES.

The annual report of the Warrington Chief , Inspector of Nuisances (Mr. Ralph Norman) which has just been issued contains a variety of informa- tion with reference to the work of his department for the year ending 31st December, 1890. He reports that during the year there have been two outbreaks of swine fever in the borough. Five Digs ' were found dead in trucks at Bank Quay Railway Station, having been smothered in transit, and these were removed to the Town Hall and buried. Mr. Norman says that during the year he has made no fewer than 112 visits to the various railway stations for the inspection of cattle trucks, pens, and gang- ways; and has upon each occasion found them in a satisfactory condition. Forty-one canal boats have been inspected; 58 samples of food submitted to the public analyst for analysis, who certified all to be genuine except One sample, which he certified to be doubtful as to its purity. There had been no evasion of the Margarine Act, and during the year 242 visits had been made to milk shops and 154 to cow- sheds. There are 81 bakehouses on the register, and three others which are not used, and they were generally found to be clean and in a satisfactory.state. There are 25 slaughter-houses on the register, and each had been regularly visited once a week. With one exception, the bye-laws for the regulation of slaughter-houses were carried out. Mr. Norman is of opinion that the estab- lishment of a public abattoir would not only simplify the labour of inspection, but conduce in the highest degree to the sanitary condition of the borough. The , tripe dressing shops have been visited weekly. Mr. ' Norman has had no complaint to make except one, and the offence consisted in keeping the tripe dressings upon the premises until they had become offensive. Seven bodies of bodies of persons who had died of infectious disease, and one body of a person unknown, who had died at the Infirmary, had been removed to the mortuary during the year. , With reference to houses visited, reported and dealt with for infringement of the lodging-house bye-laws' 574 visits have been made by the inspectors during the day and 303 by night. Table No. 4 reads as follows : Slaughter-houses within the borough, 25; bakehouses, 81 ; public urinals, 24 ;* public baths, 1; public mor- tuary, 1 ; closets on midden system, 185 ; old midden closets converted to pail system .12; water closets (about), 400; water closet converted to pail system, 1 ; common lodging-houses, 26;. houses let in lodgings,3l4 ; closets on pail system, 9,080. With reference to smoke nuisancEs, Mr. Norman reports that seven observations have been taken during the year, that seven cases have been reported,and four notices served to abate nuisances. The amount of penalties imposed by the sanitary Com- mittee is £1 is.

div.head: INHUMAN TREATMENT OF A. BOY AT HALTON. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.
div.p: INHUMAN TREATMENT OF A. BOY AT HALTON. EXEMPLARY PUNISHMENT.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. Brundritt, and Major llazlehurst, Samuel Hassall, farm labourer, of Hallwood, Halton, and his wife Mary, were 'brought up on separate informa- tions charged with having wilfully and cruelly ill- treated Samuel Roberts, age 6 years and 10 months, of whom they had the custody, in a manner likely to cause unnecessary suffering and to injure his liealth.—Mr. It. D. Maddock (Messrs. Jolliffe and , Maddock) prosecuted on behalf of the Chester Branch of the National Society f,or the Prevention ,of Cruelty to Children. In opening the case, Mr. Maddock referred to the Act under which the pro- , ceedings had been taken, and said the defendants had rendered themselves liable in a Court of Summary Jurisdiction to a fine of £25 and costs or in default or in addition thereto, three month's imprisonment. The law therefore considered he illtreatment of children a very serious offeece. The Society, which was supported by voluntary subscriptions, had no ill-feeling against the defendant, and no desire but to see justice administered. The boy Roberts was the illegitimate child of Mrs.Hassall, and there was not the slightest doubt was not looked oii with favourable eyes. He should call evidence to prove , that the child had led a miserable life, and had been neglected and illtreated in a most inhuman manner. If ' he proved this, he submitted that the defendants would not receive their deserts by the imposition of a fine; more severe punishment ought to be inflicted. After ' conviction he should ask the Bench to make an order in respect of the child. Upon their decision rested the future welfare of the child, as if he were returned to his home, he would become a vagrant—probably a criminal.—Mr. W. H. Carruthers, M.D., F.R.C.S. deposed that he ex- amined the child on the 9th inst. and found him suffering from bruises in various parts of the body. There were bruises below the right and left eye, on the left cheek, and on the left side of the lower jaw. There was a contused wound on the right templeeand on the left side of the head. There were several small bruises on the back and arms, and there was a severe and very extensive bruise on the right buttock. The wounds could not have been caused by falling down ; they appeared to be the result of blows.—Ellen Cain, a married woman cousin to the male defendant, said she lived next door to the defendants, and she had frequently heard both of them beating the boy. She had found the boy wander- ing about and afraid to go home. She had once seen the male defendant beating the child in an unmerciful man- ner with a stick.—George Gibson, 49, Portland-street, Runcorn, said on the 25th August at night, lie found the boy in Runcorn, and lie took him to a friend's house and gave him something to eat; as he appeared to be very hungry. The boy appeared loath to be taken home, and when he arrived at Halton woulEl not show witness where he lived. Eventu illy he took him home and the male defendant knocked him into the house causing him. to fall against a partition.—Margaret Rowlinson, of Halton Common, said she had seen the male defendant thrash thg boy with a stick as thick as her thumb, in a manner Ya animal ought not to be struck. When she remonstrated with him he abused her. On the follow- ing Saturday she saW the boy had a very black eye, and bruises on hisears and hands. At Christmas she also , saw him suffering from bruises.—By Hassall : She had never detained the boy on his way from school and give him" butties."—Samuel Tomlinson, school attendance officer, Halton, said the boy came to his house about ten o'clock one night in September, and he with difficulty persuaded him to go home. He had seen the boy suffer- ing from bruises, and his wrists" abraised "as though his hands had been tied with a cord.-s-P.C,. Fryer said . the boy had complained to him that his father beat him,,with a strap having a large buckle ,at the end and he had found the boy suffering from many bruises. On the 6th inst., the boy had three large scabs on his bead, bruises under both eyes, and on his body, and there were numerous discolourations. The mother said the boy had knocked his liewl against the wall, and he (witness) looked at the place, and one wound might have been caused in that way. On the 11th inst., he was 200 yards from Hallwood- Farm, when he heard a boy scream,and he went to the defendant's housea.nd walked. in. In the pantry he saw the mother holding the boy by the left hand while with her right fist she was beating him on the head and face in a most brutal manner. The boy was bleeding from the nose and ears and was black in the face. Witness had several timee warned the de- fendants as to the treatment of the boy.—John James Lonely, Inspector for the Society in the Chester District, also gave evidence as to the condition of the child.— , Hassan said he had only thrashed the boy once, and the stick spoken of by. Mrs. Rawlinson was only a twig.—The mother said the boy had only lived with her since last March. having been brought up by an old woman, and lie had had so much of his own way, that she (defendant) could not do any good with him. She could not control him in any way; he was very bad and very dirty. She had chastised him many times with her open hand, but she had never ill- treated him.—A youth named Samuel Houghton deposed that the boy cut his cheek bone through a twig he was breaking, striking him.—Mr. 13rundrit said the magis- trates considered the case was abundantly proved a.eainst both defendants. There was no doubt that they had systematically ill-treated the little boy, ard during the number of years he had sat on that Bench lie had never heard a worse case. The decision of the Bench ,was that they each pay a a fine of £5 including oasts, or a month's imprisonment.—Mr. Maddock applied that, the child should be sent to the iVorkhouse for seven days, until an industral school was found for Shim, and, Mr. Brundrit, in consenting to this request, said the Work- house would be a better home than he had had lately i Mr. Maddock: I agree with your Worship.

Caxton, --was a scholar:and a man,of affairs before he, took to printing, and seems to have been led to it by having to make sundry copies of his translation of a French version of the History of Troy.. This •viork was issued at Bruges in 1474; it was here. that Caxton- was initiated intothe mysteriesof the newly-invented art; and it,was from here that. he. • returned to England to-set up the press at West-- , minster which has made him famous for all. time:. Re died in 1491, at the age, it is. computed,. of: 70, :years, and his last printed book was appropriately entitled the "Art and Craft to die One of the earliest • books that Caxton printed was, the.. A Committee • THE Town Council of Warrington. of had under .censideration,,at their

Inquiry. last meeting, a motion to the 'effect that the Intercepting Depots should be Closed; and, as this was equivalent to capital Punishment before formal trial, it is a matter of -course to say that it was rejected!.. Since then
two notices Of motion have been sent in with a

view to dealing with the Depots.. The first is in ; the name of Councillor DixoN, and, proposes the appointment of a committee to inquire-and report to the Council as to the working of the Intercept- ing Depots, the committee to be' empowered to take such evidendi and to call to their aid' such -scientific, technical, or other testimony as may be • deemed expedient. Unfortunately the terms of: the motion exclude members of the Sanitary Committee from being members of the Committee of-Inquiry, the object, as it has been explained to 118, being to /leave the members of the Sanitary 'Committee at • liberty .to come forward and give 'evidence as -witnesses, or .as men having, a special knowledge of the working of the Depots. But • Will they- see the • matter in this light Pr We-are -afraid not. They are more likely to complain that -action is being taken. over their heads,,and resent the exclusion as a slight upon, them.. It seems to U 8 that they and the Council will be much more. likely to approve of the second notice of motion, Which has been sent in by .Councillor JENKINs. It • leaves it open to the Council,in appoikting a Special Committee, to select members of the Sanitary. asof 'Other Committees; and it differs from the. first motion in seeking to widen the scope of the in- ' Iluiry. • Councillor:JENEnis would have the. Special Committee-report not only upon the working of the Intercepting Depots," but " inquire into- and report upon the working of the Longford Depot,' With authority "to make such inquiries as may be thought desicable as to the working, of the various sanitary measures now in. force in. the borough." So far from excluding the Sanitary Committee, the co-speration of that body is "in- ' vited-with.a view to making such inquirieseibaus- tive and complete." It seems to us that the terms of this latter motion are all that can be desired for, although objection might be taken to in.clud- kg. Longford Depot .a,ud to dealing. with other "sanitary measures," it must be remembered that these things are -so co-dependent that it is scarcely Possible to touch one without trenching upon the Other. For instance, if the advisability of- closing -the Intercepting 'Depots arose out of the convic- tion that they are an incurable nuisance, it would be absolutely: necessary to consider this in its rela- tion to the manufactory at Longford, as well as in relation to ether sanitary measures. Apart from :any 'question of nuisance—though that is of-the•first importance—it is a matter for •consideration•whether the Intercepting Depots are a saving to Ahe:ratepayers, and whether, too, the Longford manufactory could not be put on such a "footing asto lessen the great drain upon the Cor- poration exchNuer which it has hitherto proved. There is no prospect of an improvement this year in its financial&ositiora. On the contrary, the fall in the -price of the manufactured article from

£6 -10 s. to NZ per ton is suggestive of the likeli- hood of &considerable loss. A private firm, under 'Buell circumstances, would be chiven to make the roost thorough investigation, with a view to reduc- 'lug the cost of production, and thus lessening the 'loss; and we-do not see why the same course should 130, t be taken because the business happens to -belong to the ratepayers. The loss at Longford d.uring the current year, will, at the lowest esti- -mate, be equivalent, if prices remain as they *are, to a rate of Twopence in the Pound, and it may turn out to be more. That is a matter, surely, to "give us pause." Then as related 'to the nuisance of the Depots, there is the ques- 'ton of the other Black Spots of Warrington,
the unpaved streets, foul drains, yards, and pas- '3agee, and wretched-tumble down houses, that are habited but "not habitable." The Reports of the Medical Officer of Health show that for many

_ Years he has been calling attention to these things, alld that, although something has been done, there 15 still a great deal to do. We observe that the ilev. JOHN YONCE made thoughtful reference to
these matters in lii. sermon on Sunday evening ; and it would be well if other ministers followed

example. We had reason to believe, after the Publ:cation of our series of articles on" The Black 'Spots of Warrington," that vigorous measures were about-to be taken to remove some of them. A resolution was come to by the Sanitary Committee to invite the Paving and Sewage Committee and Street Improvement Committee to join them in efbnferencc as to the best way of grappling with the difficulties which confronted them. This was the l'igbt course to take ; it looked like business; but, nrtfortUnately for Warrington, there has not been -a single meeting of these combined committees! Who is at fault it is not for us to say; but the fault lies somewhere. There is need for action lithere there is apathy—of energy where there is indifference; and it is therefore to be hoped that the Town Connell of Warrington will, at their next keeting, be equal to the occasion and appoint a Committee of inquiry.
Ilartlepools Election.
THE Liberal party -have bad many triumphs since tho tide turned in

favolr of Home Rule, bui, none so defimite and so cheering as that which was achieved at the Ilartlenools on Wodnesday. To convert a uxinority of 912 into a majority of 298 is at, any tibae an exd.aordinary thing; but to accomplish UIS 1I circumstances the reverse of enc ouraging :I as "Dominic Sampson" would say, "prodigious." begin with, Sir William GRAY, who was the 11°raillee of the- Tories and the Liberal Unionists, Was admitteAy 3trongest local man that could 1)038iblY 10.0 nLL;lit forward. He towered 1343ve the Liberal candidate as an employer of lab the an •I heanl his friends made the most thc) fact. More than this, he was a Liberal ynionist, it was a Liberal Unionist who, in 1886,- was returned with .ft majority of 912. Then agai), there is Cie uncertainty in Irish 'Auks has been caused by the downfall of

, Mr.. PARNELL. and yet, with the odds apparently ; so much in their favour, the so-called Unionists losetheir thumping majority, and are beaten by 298 votes!. Them is one explanation—and one • explanation only—of this splendid victory, and that is that the electors in the two Hartlepools are more than ever in favour of Home Rule. It Must be remembered that Sir WILLAist GRAW claimed to be quite as good a Liberal as Mr. C.. FtraNEss; the difference between them.was that. one. was opposed to and the other was in favour- of Home Rule. The issue was clear and unmistakable'; and. the answer is equally elearand unmistakable.. Home Rule is not dead —it is. very much alive.. Another satisfactory feature of the, contest isthe exceedingly large poll. IThere hasbeen. an. addition to the electorate since 1886 of. about 2,000 voters; but the total polled is 35058 morethan in. 1886.. All this points to the return. of. the wanderersto• the Liberal fold, and to the fact that the new electors are in the main Liberal.. The. Home Rule cause stands therefore where it. did before the division amongst the Nationalists.. If Mr. PM:NELL will only have the decency. to retirerthe triumph at the General Elec- tion will be as ‘great as that of the Hartlepools.

Replying to a correspondent as to the probabi- lity of a general election. taking place shortly, Lord Sashayy says he has a° ground for believing that an eariy dissolution is probable. Precisely; a change has come o'er- the spirit of the dream; a series of Itartlepods,, at a General Election, would be a whirlpool for the Tory party.

Mr., Parnell still continues to condemn himself by railing at wha.t he calls "Mr. Uladstone's whittled down measure of Home Rule." If the ex-leader refers to the Bill of 1885,: the answer is that he voted for it; if to the measure considered at the Hawfirden interview, the answerin that case is that he afterwards again and again expressed his satisfaction with the results of that interview. Mr. Parnell is impaled on the horns of a dilemma, and his loud cries simply attract attention to a position which is as dishonourable as it is lament- able.

The Tories are quite angry now that they are beginning to realise that the fall of Mr. Parnell does not mean the fall of Home Rule. The "Morn- ing Post" calls upon the Opposition to proclaim a policy, or admit that it has ceased to advocate Home Rule. If that very aristocratic organ were not as stupid as the party it represents, it would perceive that the advocacy of Home Rule is in it- self the proclamation of a policy. But if the "Morning Post" wants to put " posers" let it ask Lord Salisbury when he means to carry out his policy, and redeem his pledges by granting local self-government to Ireland.

In the course of his speech at Cambridge, Lord Salisbury said :—" Even if Mr. Morley's anticipa- tion of obtaining a majority at the next election should be justified, which does not look very likely at the present moment, then it would be an absurd examration to say that• Home Rule would than have been victorious. There is position after posi- tion to be carried long before they could reach auch an end as that." That is to say the house of Lords would throw out the Home Rule Bill; and . what could be better? It would give the people the opportunity of throwing out the House of Lords.

The " Times" is making a fuss over the alleged discovery of a lost work by Aristotle on the consti- tutional history of Athens. It relates to events some six hundred years before the birth of Christ, and is said to throw light on "the lamentable social and commercial condition of Attica." But what matters? We have been overdosed and surfeited with ancient Greece. The problem to-day is the lamentable social condition of England; light upon that is what is wanted. We cannot get excited about fresh details as to the condition of Attica 2,400 years ago. What's Attica to us or us to Attica, that we should weep for it? Besides, it may yet transpire that the find is a forgery.

Whilst special interest is being taken in the cure of consumption as the result of Dr. Koch's experi- ments, attention may usefully be directed to Mr. G. T. Congreve's treatment which has in many cases been very successful. His book on consump- tion and other chest diseases is well worth read- ing. It contains valuable instructions as to auxi- liary treatment, with important chapters on diet, air, exercise, &c. It contains, too, an interesting record of a large number of selected eases. It may be had, post free, for one shilling, from the author, Coombe Lodge, Peckham, London, S.E.

A special census which has been made in the United States shows that Jewish population are not increasing in proportion to the rest of the com- munity. The birth-rate is, in fact, ten per cent. lower than the average ; and it transpires that, contrary to the usual order of things, it is the poorer classes who have the fewest children. It is suggested that the falling off is to be accounted for by a low marriage rate, and increased ago of mar- riage. Voltaire once said of the sons of Abraham that they were noted for two things—getting money and children. It would appear that they are now losing one of their characteristics.

The Cheshire Standing Joint Committee were usefully occupied, on Saturday,in inquiring into the miscarriage of justice which has resulted through thee magistrates of Nantwich failing to defend their decision in the case of. a licensinm, appeal. It would seem that the Magistrates' Clerk was at fault iv neglecting to call the Bench together, and thus getting their instructions. The police were represented at the appeal, but they were helpless under the circumstances, and a -more humiliating spectacle it is hafdly possible to conceive—to say nothing of the needless expense.. The matter is being .pursued further, as it should be; the magis- trates are to be asked for an explanation,- and there is talk of bringing the Clerk to book by a motion to reduce his salary.

A RUNCORN NAVVY AND MS WIFE.

• Before Mr. Handley and Dr. Steele at Runcorn Court, on Tuesday, James Rogers, a ship canal navvy living in Ellesmere-st., was charged with threatening his wife Charlotte on the 23rd October. The prisoner had been summoned to answer the charge on the 10th November, but he did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. The police had been unable to execute it until the present time. It was stated that the prisoner is a man of very drunken habits and had been before the magistrates of Oswestry, to which he belonged, over 20 times. His wife declined to press the present charge against him, and the Bench bound him over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered him to pay the costs
KINDNESS ILL-REQUITED AT RUNCORN.

On Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, a boy named James Buxton (11) was charged with stealing 2s. belong- ing to Mary Elizabeth Woods of Canal-st. About a , month ago Mrs. Woods gave shelter to the boy who was I homeless and wandering about the neighbourhood. On the 12th she sent him to fetch half a pound of mutton chops for her husband's dinner and also half a gallon of paraffin oil. She gave him 2s. with which to pay for the articles, and he never returned. Afterwards P.C. Wood- row apprehended the boy, who said he had used the.. money to go to his aunt's at Simms Cross, Widnes. The. magistrates sentenced the wisoner to 21 days imprison-- ment and afterwards to be ,'.--confined in a reformatory for. five years.

Dr. Crcss further urged that it was a hardship to the girls to be turned out of doors; and so it would be if there were no places for them to go to; but as a matter of fact there are rur fewer than nine Homes in Liverpool for fallen ' women and girls.

Mr. Quilliam appeared before the Committee on behalf of other shopkeepers; but he agreed with the • chairman that in a matter of morality pecun- iary consideration should not be taken into account. He sought to make it out that it was best for the social and moral health of the community that the women should be undisturbed. To turn them out was to increase street solicitation,and distribute the traffic over the city. There is a point in this, but it is a point which might be made in opposition to rooting out a theives' quarter, or receivers of stolen goods. The clear course is for the Committee to do what is right in enforcing the law. They must, as far as they can, make it easy to do right, and hard to do wrong—but it is not every Watch Com- mittee that has the courage to take such a course.

div.head: TIIE AGED. PERSONS TREAT AT' RIJNOAIRN. .
div.p: TIIE AGED. PERSONS TREAT AT' RIJNOAIRN. .

A meetin of the General Committee of tbi4 teat was held at the Town Hall,. an Wednesday evening, tuider•the presidency of Mr, Samuel Taylor, There was a capital attendatice„—Mr„ H, Wright (one of the ban, secttetaries), wad the report of the Commit- tee, vihiasaid it was highly gratifying to. record the liberality with. which the public had responded to the appeal for help, bath with money and 'goods.. The Committee pointed out that the idea af reviv- ing the treat originated with the Rev. Joseph Holden, and reviewed the work of gin various corn- , mittees engaged in organising the treat. The num- ber of tickets issued was 539, and in addition invalids numbering 6.6 received packets containing a quarter lb. of tea, half a lb, of sugar, half a lb. of butter, one ounce of tobacco, two mince pies and two oranges. They begged to accord their thanks to Mrs. C. Hazlehurst for the loan of plants; Mrs, GorEit and Messrs. Mellor and Spearing for cooking meat; Messrs. Yarwood; Jackson and Brereton for the loan of cabs; Messrs. 1, Stubbs, W. Hankinson. T. Reynolds and Mrs. Lea for Carting; Mr. J. W. Timperley for loan of piano; Captain Le Couteur for decorating the Hall ; and to all the ladies and gentle- men who assisted at the entertainment; to the Co-operative Society, Foresters' Club and the vari- otis school managers for the loan of tables and tea ems; to . the ladies who presided at the tables, and to the ladies and gentlemen who assisted in cutting up the food. It was hoped that the treat having been so successful this year would become one of the permanent institutions of the town. (Applause.)—A balance sheet was also presented, showing that the receipts amounted to £75 19s. id. including." a balance of £9 4s. id. from the treat of 1888. The expenditure, amounted to £39 14s. 11d., leaving a balance of £3B 4s. 2d. in the hands of the hon. treasurer (Mr. J. C. Holland.)—The report and balance sheet were adopted and a discussion took place as to the disposal of the balance.—Mr. W. Littler mbved that it remain in the hands of the trea.sibrer and Captain Le Couteur proposed that it be banded over to the Relief Fund Committee at once.—The ' Chairman re- marked that the ttelief Committee had funds to carry them on for the next few days,but if.,the frost continued they would require all the help they could get. He therefore suggested that the Treat Committee should re- main in existence, and meet for the purpose of disposing of the balance in the course of a few days. Eventually it. was derided that the Committee be called together at the discretion of the Chairinan.e-A long discussion ensued as to the advisability of advertising the balance sheet and the list of subcribers, and a motion to do so was negatived. A proposal was made by Dr. Gastaldi to send a balance sheet to all subscribers over ten shillings and Mr. ReynOlciB moved that subscriber of 53. and over be provided wittra sheet. Mr. .Smith made a further proposition that each person who had contributed Eid. be supplied.—Mr. Littler,ineved that unless the Whole of the subscribers were supplied no balande sheets be 'sent out at all, and the proposition being seconded by Mr. J. B. Ltolland was carried. No balance sheets will therefore be distributed.—Dr. Gastaldi said he observed at the tea that some of the old men and women could not enjoy their sandwiches, and he hoped next year they would substitute something they could more easily masticate. Mr. Hewitt thought the tea and everything went off adm:rably. If they had to buy teeth for these old people, they would get into a difficulty. The sandwiches were splendid, he tried them himself. (Laughter.) They could not make food that wOuld suit everybody.—The subject tnen drOpped.---Mr. Howitt prqposed a vote of thanks ti the Chairman (Mr. Taylor), te the lion. secs. (Messes. J. P. juries, H. Wright, and W. B. Frith), and to the hon. treasurer (Mr. ; lioditnd), for the admirable manner in which • they had worked to make the treat a success.—t)r. Gastaldi seconded, and the Rev. A. Finch Supported the motion, which was Carried imanimously.—ln riply the Chairman sold in all his experience he had never met with anything that had been brought forward in Runcorn, that had been taken up so heartily by everyone ; and those who had undertaken the work were quite recompensed by the success Which had attended the treat.—The Secretary and Treasurer also responded.—The Chairman, in bring- ing the meeting to a close said after the interest aroused in the treat it would be Utterly impossible for it to fall through again. It should go forth to the public, that whoever occupied the position of Chairman of the Board of Commiisioners, would be expected to bring this, WM.

div.head: DEATH FROM AI.VOHOLISM AT iVIDNES.
div.p: DEATH FROM AI.VOHOLISM AT iVIDNES.

An inquest was held by Mr. Husband, the deputy coroner, at Widnes Police Court on Tuesday morning,on the body of a labourer named John Quinn, ok 27, Catherine-st., who diad suddenly on Saturday last, It appeared that about a year ago the deceased was sent to Bainhill Asylum i consequence of his drinking habits. He was set at liberty at the end of a few manths and since then he had been drunk almost every day. At two o'clock on Satarday afternoon he sent oat for a pint of beer which he. drank. At half past four he lay down on the sofa and. apparently went to sleep,, but an hour later when his.-.aaother tried to rouse him, she found that he was dead. He was 31 years of age. The jury re- turned a verdict of death from " Alcoholism." UNIVE.P.AITY EXTENSION LECTO RES. AT RUNCORN. The second series of lectures this winter, under.tho. auspices of the Oxford Extension Scheme was com- menced Bethesda Lecture Hatt on Friday last week, ' when rilr. H. J. Mac Kinder, M. A. (reader in geography in the University of Oxford, delavered the first lecture on , "The growth of the political system of Europe." The title of the course is" The Mating of Nations." The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood introduced, the lecturertwho said he hoped the course of lectures they were entering upon would prove interesting and instructive. The science of politics he explained had nothing in common with, party politics, and he defined a nation as a body of people who in habits acted together for political purposes. No one would deny that the Swiss were a nation, and a very patriotic nation; yet some Swis.s talked French, some German, and some Italian and some did not talk any of the three. They might have a nation of people who talked different languages, and they might have been two separate nations such:as the American and the English, which although speaking the same tongue, did not act politically together. Europe was composed of a number of indepedent states, which might be said to form a domestic family, because they resembled one another far more than they resemble any other nation on the earth,. in religion, law, language, history, arts and social cus- toms. But they had rival interests and ambitions, which brought conflict with one another, and the lecturer e::- plained at length how these disputes were settled by diplomacy and war, and both of these implied an inter- national law. We English at the present time were ashamed of certain things which had gone on in Central Africa, and learned that there was no moral law which was really supported by international law. By means of maps thrown on a screen by a lantern manipulated by Mr. H. W. Handley, the lecturer entered into details of the European political system, ind the manner in which it was influenced by the whole of Southern Asia.

The annual CC-ngregational bea party in connection with Runcorn Parish Church was held on Monday even- ing, at the National School. The donations towards the tea were as numerous as ever, and a large company sat down to the excellent repast provided. Afterwards a concert took place under the presidency of the vicar, the Rev. Canon Wood, and the proceedings derived addi- tional interest from the presence of Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool. During an interval in the programme Mr. Aspinall delivered a speech, in which he apologised for not keeping his appointment to attend the recent bazaar, and said the large attendance that evening looked hope- ful as well as helpful, for the parish. He had known Canon Wood for many years, and when he heard that he was coming to Runcorn he (Mr. Aspinall), knew that the Runcorn people would never have cause to regret the appointment. (Applause.) He understood there were four curates in the parish, and he was sure there was lots of work for them to do. It was a disadvantage to a parish if it were starved in the matter of clergy help, and in his opinion there was no parochial system in the world like the English system if it were properly sup- ported and carried out as it ought to be. (Applause.) Ile urged them to give greater help to their clergy, and drew their attention to several societies worthy of sup- port. If church people would only give and would try to lessen the number of points of difference and dis- agreement, and increase the points upon which they could agree, the church would be mose harmonious than 'it was at the present moment. (Applause.) Let them bring people to be a more social, kindly, friendly, and to use a Lancashire word, cosy family. (Applause.) In conclusion he promised to visit Runcorn in Lent, and and deliver a speech on temperance. On the proposi- tion of Mr. J. E. Meredith, seconded by the Rev. J. Holden, a cordial vote of thanks was awarded to Mr. • Aspinall for his address. The following programme was gone through :—Glee " The holly crown'd king," Run- corn Parish Church choir ; song " Sons of freedom," Master Challis; duet " Brotherly love," Messrs. Littler and Wilkinson ' • song " Bay of Biscay," Mr. Garner ; solo (cornet) " Star of Bethlehem," (encore). Mr. R. W. Pierpoint ; glee" The home land," choir ; sohg Robin Adair," (encore) Miss Wright ; song " Jerusalemr" Mr. Caygill ; address by Clarke Aspinall, Esq., J.P. ; glee "The old brigade," choir ; song "Steering home," Mr. Wilkinson ; solo (coronet) "Daughter of the Regiment," (Donizetti) Mr. R. .W. Pierpoint ; song " The sea is England's glory," Master Done ; song "Mona," Mr. C. Pownall ; solo (pianoforte) " Scherzo," (Beethoven) 'Mist Augusta Jones; song "Nazareth," Mr. Gates ; glee "The -Village Blacksmith," choir; "God save the Queen," (solo by Master F. Bradley.) The usual vote of thanks concluded the concert. Clamart, High Clags Tailor, Bold-at. Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WIDLIES PUBLICAN AT FAUIT.
div.p: A WIDLIES PUBLICAN AT FAUIT.

On Thursday, at the Widnes-Petty Sessions, Ellis Sankey. landlord of the Queen's Arms Motel, Moor- lane, was charged-on a summons with. having sold intoxicating-drink during prohibited hours„and two others, named Arthur Owen and Arthur lienyon, both of Moor-lane, were summoned for having been on licensad:premises during prohibited hours. Evi- dence waagiven by Constable Almond to-the effect that shortly after midnight on Saturday he saw Owen arod- Kenyon go ints),the yard of the Queen's Arms Ifttel. One of tilem tapped at the window. Mrs. Sankey thereupon came to the door and asked who was there. She received the reply "Arthur," and then let the men into the house. Witness ap- proached the window,,and saw that the lights were turned down. He could, however,, observe what took place by tlte light of the fire. The three defendants were sitting near the fire, and drink: was supplied to them. Some was paid for by Kaeroyon, and the larxilord said that he would pay font-he remainder.—Other witnesses having been ciifled, Sankey said that the other two defendants I were Invited gues..4-3,and no drink was paid for them. When they came to, the door, he invited them to .reniain to supper.. .k,sked by the superintendent of the police if the-invitation had been given before they came to the house, he replied in the negative. —Owen said ha went to the hotel to obtdin some • brandy for a al& person, and Kenyon said he ac- companiedOwen.—The magistrates considered the case proved. They fined Owen and Kenyon 10s. and costs each, and in regard to the landlord a fine of 4,05. and costs was imposed. As it was his first ogence they would not endorse the license, but they thought the case a very bad one.

YR.srmtney.—Before Judge Shand. Damacys FOR Loss 01, A HORSR.—John Clare, of the Ring O'Bells, Farnworth, sued Frederick Simcock, of the Black Horse, Farnworth, for the sum of £2l las. 6d., damages, for injury to the plaintiff's horse, from which it died, through the careless, improper, and negligent driving of the defendant. Mr. J. 0. Swift was for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Knowles for the defendant. The case occupied three hours in hearing, - but the facts shortly are as follows :—On the 12th September, the plaintiff's horses were being driven home down School- lane, from the field where they had been drawing a mowing machine. They were in charge of a boy, who, seeing the defendant driving towards him at a very rapid rate, attempted to take his horses out of the way, but before he could do so, the defendant's trap had col- lided with one of the animals, the shaft of the trap pene- trating its chest to the depth of five inches. The hope was placed under the care of a veterinary, surgeon, but died from the effects of its in- juries. The defence was that the defendant was driving in a careful manner, and at a steady space, but that the boy oould not control the horses he was in charge of.—The Judge gave a verdict for the plaintiff for £l4, with costs. THE THEXTRE OF VARIETIES.—AIfred Edwards, Widnes- road, sued Daniel Cohen, of the Theatre of Varieties for Ell 19s. 3d., being the balance of an account for printing Scc., Mr. Peters appeared for the plaintiff.—The defend- ant admitted his liability in part, but said several of the items had been incurred by companies acting at the theatre for which he was not lihle.H Honour gave judgment for £7 7s. 9d. to be paid in monthly instal- ments of El.

METHODIST FREE CHURCH.—A public meeting was held in the above church on Monday evening, when a lecture on" The Life and Times of John Wesley " was delivered by the Rev. 11. Fothergill. Mr. Thomas Rigby, Of Sutton Weaver, presided. HOME MtssioNs.---Sermons on behalf of the Wesleyan, Home Missions were preached in the Trinity Chapel„l Frodsham, on Snnday last ; in the morning by the Rev. F. F. Edmunds, and evening by Mr. S. Woodward. 'l‘.he annual public meeting was held on Tuesday evenings, the' chair being occupied by Mr. Isaacs, when the, Rev, J. H. Hopkins, of the London Mission, attended as the, deputation, and gave a thrilling account of the work in which he is engaged in the Southwark district of the Mission. The Rev. P. Pizey also addressed the meeting. JUVENILE PRACTICAL JOKING ON THE SI-ITP CANA.L.---At Prodsham Police Court, on Thursday, a boy named John Samuel Fletcher was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to Fred. Neil and William Haigh,, his com- panions. On the morning of the 3rd January the boys were in a hut on the Ship Canal, at Frodsham Marsh, and Neil scattered the fire with a hammer. Then find- ing a number of "old stocking feet," he threw them on the hot cinders, and the stench that arose drove Haigh and Fletcher out, Neil remarking that he could stand more thamthat. Fletcher said "I'll fetch him out, and walked away. Haigh returned into the hut. In a few minutes Fletcher returned with a %ticket containing lucigen oil,and he poured it down the chimney. At once the hut was filled with fire and sraoke, and Haigh and Neil had some difficulty in finding the door. When they emerged Neil's face was black and blistered, and his clothes were on fire. A workman, extinguished the flames, 14ut not before he was badly burnt. Haigh was also severely burned on the hands. Roth were conveyed on an engine to the hospital,' at Ellesmere Port. For some days Neil's lifeswas in great danger, and he is still an inmate of the hospital, and Dr. Benstock informed the bench he was likely to bo for another fortnight. Haigh was under treatment for a fortnight. The bench com- mitted Fletcher to the quartec sessions for trial.

PARA'S BANEING COMPAN Y, LIMITED.
ANNUAL MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS.

The annual meeting of the eNareholders of Parr's Banking Company. Limited, Vna held at the bank premises, Winwick-st., I'Varringtelt, yesterday. Mr. J. C. Parr Presided, and the other directors present were Colonel Gamble, C.D., Mr. E,...e=renall. Mr. A. Hewlett, Mr. G. 3lcCorquodale, Si :r T. G. Frost, Mr. A. Turner, .Mr. Cecil F. Parr. Wllen" was a good attendance of shareholders. - THE DIEECTORS' HEPORT:.• •

The Directors' report to the meeting read. as follows: —" The Directors, in submitting to the shareholders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. By the issue to the shareholders of 2,000 new shares in terms of reso- lution passed on 25th July, and confirmed 22nd August, 1890, the subscribed capital of the Company has been increased from £2,800,000 to £3,000,000, the paid up capital from £560,000 to £600,000; and the reserve fund from £300,000t0 £360,000. The new shares do not take dividend until }midsummer. Including --£25,203-3S. sd. brought from previous account, the net balance- of pro- fits, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five per cent., is £151,715 4s. Bd. The distribution of this sum, recommended by the Directcrs, is as follows : Interim half-year's dividend of nine per cent., declared 25th July, £50,400; dividend to be now paid of nine per mat., free of income tax, making 18 per cent, for the year, £50,400; bonus of 4s. per share (one per cent.), free of income tax, £5,600; to writedown to 90 £65,000 consols recently purchased, £3,113; to reserve fund— raising it to £.370,000, £10,000; to property account, £5,000; balance to next account, £27,206 4s. Bd. On the suggestion of the Bank of England, the directors have to the extent of £150,000, joined with the leading London, Provincial, and Scottish Banks, in the guarantee against loss to the Bank of England in the liquidation of of the estrte Baring Bros. and Co., which, with admir- able promptitude and decision, that bank undertook in November last, thereby averting a panic which would have had a disastrous effect on banking and general credit. The directors hope that the liquidation will be effected without loss to the guarantors. The directors

whc retire at this time by rotation are Mr. Peter Stubs, ' Colonel Gamble, C. 8., Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Bart.,. Mr. Henry Woodcock, and Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley, all a whom are recon2.mended for re-election. Sub-branches have been opened at Ashton-in-Makerfield, Haydock, Lymna, and Sutton. The articles of associatidn of the company are without the power usual in the case of joint stock banks, to compel executors or administrators of deceased shareholders to transfer the shares of the deceased holder from his name. In order to prevent an increasing number of the company's shares from remaining in the names Of deceased holders, the directors propose that the special resolution of which due notice is herewith given should -be passed, prescribing that the dividends or profits on the shares of a deceased member shall, unless the directors in their uncontrolled discretion otherwise appoint, be retained until such shares are duly registered in another name." The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report,. said it was a great matter of congratulation both to the directors and shareholders that they had still the same tale to tell of uninterrupted prosperity. The balance they had to show was one of the strongest, if not the strongest, they had ever had the satisfaction of bringing before the annual meeting. (Applause.) They never,- appreciated safety more than when danger threatened, and although the danger might have been distant and could only possibly have affected them indirectly, still U ter have every reason to be pleased and thankful that it. had been averted. Of course they would understand that he alluded to the commercial crash, which at one time seemed imminent and unavoidable,when the great house of Baring Brothers was unable to meet its engagements and was on the brink of suspension. Great emergencies. called for hereic remedies, and fortunately there was at the head of the Bank of England a man who was. prompt enough and strong enough to grasp the situation, and be called to his counsel the heads of great banking firms and financial institutions—having first satisfied himself by preliminary investigation that the house of Baring Brothers, although for the moment hopelessly in.- volved and paralysed, was still not insolvent—and at once undertook to be responsible for all their liabilities. In order to support the Bank of England in this prompt and praiseworthy action, a numbei of London banks and monetary institutions joined in the guarantee to hold them harmless, however a liquidation might result, and that guarantee speedily reached the very large figure of £17,000.000, the bank of England heading the list with £1,000,000. Subsequently provincial banks, their own amongst the number, were invited to join that guaran- tee and feeling the promptitude of the action and the magnitude of the crisis averted, they very liber- ally responded to the appeal, and that bank's name- was added to the number to the figure of £ISC,GOO.- As their report told them, it was hoped that none of that money would be required, but that the. assets. of Baring Brothers would be sufncient to cover, their liabilites. Having quoted a reported statement- of the governor of the bank of England that probably no claim would be made on the guarantors, the Chairman added that the governor of the bank of England had re-iterated that statement to their general manager (Mr. Dun), so lately as Tuesday last. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to other parts of the report, he said the business of the bank con- tinued in every way satisfactory. There was a marked increase in the accounts, and the increase 'ass very equally distributed over the whole area of the bank's district.

Colonel MCCORQIIODALE seconded the Chairman's pro- posal that the report be adopted, and after a question had been answered as to the value of the bank's pro- perty, the motion was passed unanimously.

A resolution was then passed in femur of the payment of a dividend as recommended by the,directors. On the of Captain WITHINGTON it was also agreed to thank the directors for tkeir services. duting the past year, and to give them a remuneration of £S,COG. for the year now begun.—The retiring directors, az. mentioned in the report, were re-elected on the motion of Major Pickinere. —On the motion of Mr. H. MlLL:szr, seconded by Mr.. D. GAaserr, Mr. J. C. Stead, of Liverpool, was re-elected auditor at a salary of £400.. Mr. STEAD, in acknowledg- ing the appointment, spoke of theozeuracy of the balance sheet that was submitted to-the shareholders.—A. vote of thanks was, on the . motion. of Mr. JOHN Wnlynt, accorded the general mluager. . John Dun), the secre- tary (Mr. Murray) and the other ofEcers for their services, and was acknowledged by Mr. Dun. AN EXTRAbRDINAEY cekiNEEtAL MEETING.

An extraordinary general meeting was then held for the purpose of passing the following resolution :--" That the; Articles of Association of the-empany be altered. by the insertion therein of the following article, namely 114.t.—The dividend, extraordinary dividend, or bonus payable upon shares. in respect of which any person. is, under the Company's articles.relating ta the transfer and transmission of shares, entitled to become a number, or- which any person under those articles isentitled to trans- fer, shall, unless the Directors in -their uncontrolled dis- cretion otherwise appoint, be retained until such person. shall become a member in respect of such shares, or shall duly transfer the same, sad every transier on such shares shall carry with it all dividends, extraordinary dividends, or bonuses which may have been retained as herein pro- vided."--The resolution was passed without aiscu.ssion on the proposal of the Casimtx, seconded. by Colonel GAmin,E.
A vote of thanks t> the Chairman brc.ught the.rnpeting to a close.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Ti* NUISANCE COMPLAINED OF BY COUNCILLOR DIXON. Thomas McGuire and William Richardson, were charged with being disorderly, on the night of the 19th inst., in Sankey-st. The offence consisted of that recently complained of to the Bench by Councillor Dixon, and was committed near his house.—Alderman Harrison said it was a nuisance that ought to be put a stop to.—John Smallwood, was charged with the like offence close by in Arpley-st., on the same night. The Wree defendants were fined the costs, 3s. 6d. each, but the Bench intimated that in future such cases would be dealt with much more severely. STEALING FROM A CLOTHES LINE.

At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, Sarah Gavin and Mary McComb, of 4, Friars-lane, were charged with stealing from the back yard of John Bolton, 7, Clare-st., a blue flannel, value 2s. 6d., or receiving the same knowing it to have been itolen.—llarriet Bolton deposed that on Wednesday night, about 6.30, she missed the singlet from the line. She identified the singlet produced.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said. he in company with Constable Smith went to McComb's house and asked her about the singlet. At first she said she knew nothing about it, but he brought her to the Police Station, an.l she said she had bought a singlet for 4d. from Mrs. Gavin, who had sent out for two pints of beer for the 4d. Gavin was also taken into custody.— Gavin who now made her 23rd appearance, her previous -conviction having been for stealing a singlet, was now committed for a month's harp labour; and there being a doubt in M.rs, Comb's case, the Bench gave her thetbene- fit of it, and discharged her.
CI-URGES OF THEFT.

On Monday before the Mayor (Alderman W. Fran- comb), and Aldermen-Harrison, Sutton, and Davies, John Jones, fireman of Liverpool, and Thomas Russell, an assistant in the model lodging house Old-road, who also comes from Liverpool, were charged with stealing from the shop of Wm. Coates, draper, Friars Gate, on Satur- day last, six cotton shirts, value 7s. 6d.—Mr. Coates indentified shirts produced, as five of the six stolen.— Edward Coates son of the prosecutor, said he saw the shirts all right at the door about half-past six, and missed them about seven. Information was then given to the police.—Mrs. Gibbons, dealer, Mersey-street, deposed that on SatuKday night Russell came to her with a shirt and asked 2s. for it. She gave him is. Bd. for it, and he went away. Presently Detective-Sergeant Monaghan came in about a pair of trousers she had bought, and while he was there the prisoner Jones entered, and offered a shirt for sale. Monaghan subse: quently took him into custody.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan corroborated the latter statements, and said Jones told him that he had just given 3s. 9d. for the shirt at Coates's in Bridge-st. Witness told him it was a strange thing for him to buy a shirt for 3s. 9d. and then immediately after want to sell it for 2s. and brought him to. the police station, where Mr. Coates's man identified the shirt as one of the six. On witness charging the prisoner he said a man had given it .to him in Walker's vaults. Witness brought the other prisoner away from the model lodging house, and when Jones saw Russell he said he was the man who gave him the shirt. Russell replied "Yes, lam the man who gave him the shirt. I bought it in a pawn shop in Liverpool." Witness subsequently found three other shirts in the back yard of the lodging-house.—The prisoners were sent for a month's hard labour each.—Henry Russell, a painter from Liverpool, living'at a lodging-house in Rose and Crown-st., was then charged with stealing from the shop-door of Ann Ja.ckson, pawnbroker, Winwick-st., en Saturday afternoon, a pair of trousers, value 6s. 11d. It appeared that Detective Sergeant Monaghan had ascer- tained that the prisoner had pawned the trousers at Mrs. Leslie's for 4s. He returned there on Sunday and pur- chased a pair of trousers for 7d. Monaghan having in the meantime been making inquiries about the prisoner, Mrs. Leslie detained him and sent for Monaghan,and on his arrival gave the man into custody.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and sobbingly exclaimed that he had committed the theft because he was simply starving. He had walked, he said, all the way from Liverpool, and eaten nothing for four days. He was committed for amonth's hard labour. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Mary Williams, who has been residing with her husband at a lodging-house in Market-st., was charged with steal- ing on the 19th inst., from the shop of Messrs. Robertson and Son, clothiers, Buttermarket-st , one pair of tweed trousers, value Bs. 11d.—C1ieif Constable Hunt said on the trousers being missed from the door of the shop a policeman was sent for, and as the prisoner had been seen to leave the door of the shop he followed her and found that she was carrying the trousers under her shawl. She was brought to the. olice station and charged, and her reply was that she would not have done it, but she was in want. It turned out that she and her husband were in a poverty-stricken state. Her husband was very ill in bed, and an order had been given for his removal to the workhouse that day.—P.C. Bruen deposed to the cir- cumstances under which he apprehended her.—The prisoner said her husband was a quarryman, but had not worked fez' four months, having been ill for that period, suffering from' inflammation of the lungs. She and her husband came from Patricroft. She had asked the relieving officer yesterday if he could assist her.—P.C. Bruen said the prisoner and her husband had been receiving 13s. a week for some time from Mr. Walker, and at present had ss.a week.—The prisoner said she had never received 135., only 10s. a week. Her husband was now in the Ship Canal club and receiving ss. a week from it, but she had 4s. Bd. to pay out of it for lodgings. —P.C. Bruen said Dr. Peacock had visited her husband, and said he would see to him being conveyed to the workhouse.—The Chairman said the best plan would be for the prisoner to go there too, and she replied that she wished she could.—The Chairman: We shall record the conviction against you, but not punish you under the circumstances. But you will be liable to be called up for it if there is anything else.
THEFTS FROM TRADESMEN.

At the Warrin—gtou Borough Police Cou- rt, on Wednes- day, before Alderman Holmes and Mr. J. Fairclough, Michael Burke and Wm. Jones were charged with steal- ing on the 19th inst., 10lbs. of brisket beef, value 4s. 2d., the property of:Arthur linutt Hodstan,.butcher, 92 Mer- sey-st.—The prosecutor deposed to missing the brisket on the afternoon of the 19th, having seen it on his board a few minutes before.—John McGuinness, deputy at Mrs. Mulholland's lodging house, a few doors from the. prose- cutor's said the two prisoners had been lodging there. Ile was standing leaning over the wall at the back of the lodging house on Tuesday afternoon, and saw them come out of the house and after some conversation go to the butcher's, Jones brought something away from the butcher's board., which appeared like meat;and he gave it to Burke. They came up to the lodging house door, and he ordered themoutint,o the street. They bothwent towards Bridge Foot, and in about three quarters of an hour, they brought some bread and bacon home for tea. He gave information to Mr. Hudston.—P.S. Rowbotham said about 10 minutes past eight on Tuesday night Mr. Hudston informed him about the men stealing his meat. He apprehended them. Burke was very abusive and refused to give his nathe, but Jones gave his. Witness brought them to the police stition, and on searching them found a knife on Burke, and 7d. on Jones.—Jones in reply to the Bench, said he came from Oldham where his parents lived.—Burke was committed for a month's and Jones for a fortnight's hard labour. At the War- rington Borough Police Court on Thursday, before Major Litton (chairman), Captain Ridgeway, and Alderman Sutton, the prisoners Burke and Jones were again brought

up, charged with stealing on Tuesday afternoon from the shop of Messrs. Robertson and Sons, drapers, Butter- bid market-st., & navvy's vest, val 6s. 6d.—Robert Rod- well, manager to Messrs. Ro tson and Sons, deposed that just before 4 o'clock on Tuesday afternoon he saw Burke near the shop, and missed the vest shortly after. —Robert Cook said he saw Burke lift the vest.off a hook at the shop door, and go away followed by Jones.—P.C. Rowbottom said he saw the priscners hanging about the shop shortly before four o'clock, and soon after received information of the robbery. He apprehended the pri- soners and charged ttlem with stealing the waistcoat. On being charged Burke said " I have never stole any waist- coat as I know of. I have been drinking beer all day." Jones replied, "I know nothing about it."—Burke now said he was not accountable for what he had done. He had been drinking beer all day, and did not know whether he took the waistcoat or not.—Jones said he was with Burke part of the day, but he was drunk, and they quarrelled, and parted.—P.C. Hardy said he saw the prisoners together during the afternoon, several times.—Claief Constable Hunt mentioned that Burke was a native of Hull, and a ship stoker.—The Chairman said it seemed very evident that the prisoners had come to Warrington to live upon what plunder they could get. His colleagues were more lenient than he was, and he gave way to them. Burke was sentenced to a month's, and Jones to a fortnight's, imprisonment, with hard labour.—The Chief Constable said the night before last there had been four robberies from shop doors, and these offences were very much on the increase just now. —The Chairman said the Bench had had cases cf this kind betore them very often lately, and expressions of opinion had been made to them that the tradespeople were very careless in exposing their goods, and that to a great extent it served them right 'to lose them. Tradesmen really had no right to expose their goods, but the bye-laws were not sufficiently strong to prevent .them. The police could only do what they could tO catch the thieves, but if they could not, tradesmen must take the consequences of their own folly.—Alder- man Sutton said the exposure of goods was certainly a great temptation, and tradespeople ought to try to pro- tect themselves in a great measur3 from these thieves by not exposing their goods in the way they did at their doors.—Mr.'Rodwell said in this case the goods were not exposed outside, but were three feet within their door.— Alderman Sutton: You don't expose your goods out- side ?—Mr. Rodwell : We don't during the week, but we do so on Saturdays.—The Chief Constable said the general answer of tradesmen was that it was done in Manchester and Liverpool, and if they did not do it they would do no business. Mr. Hunt also drew attention to the fact that most of these robberies from shop doors were committed by strangers.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair) Councillor Voisey, and Mr. Robert Garnett. THEFT OF A WATCH AND CHAlN.—Maurice Burns. a puddler, employed at Bewsey Forge, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of John Allen, 122, Catherine-st., on Friday afternoon a silver lever watch, value £lO, and a silver chain vallie £2. The prisoner who had been without regular employment for some time, was engaged by Mr. Allen to chip some bricks. On the afternoon in question the prisoner went into Mr. Allen's house for some tea or coffee. The watch was in the cupboard when the prisoner went in. John Allen, a son of the prosecutor, saw him go to the cupboard, the prisoner saying he was looking for a match. He left the house shortly afterwards, and the watch and chain were almost immediately missed. The prisoner, it appears, ' went to Mr. Houghton's pawnshop in Mersey-st., and offered the watch and chain in pledge for 12s. In I answer to questions from the assistant, the prisoner said he brought the watch from Liverpool, but gave sixpence for the chain in the market. This aroused the assistant's suspicions, and a policeman was sent for.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge.—The Chairman said the Bench were perfectly satisfied that the prisones had committed the theft, and considering the kindness he had received from Mr. Allen and the abuse of that kindness, they considered that he was deserving of a severe sentence. Tie would be committed to goal for three months with hard labour. The Chairman added that the conduct of the pawnbroker's assistant was most. priiseworthv, _ _ _

YESTERDAY.—Before Mr. J. White (Chairman) Alderman

Harrison and Dr. GOrnall. • UNLAWFULLY QurrTING SERVICE.—EIIen Ogden, of 18, Dutton-st., an apprentice, was charged with absenting herself from the service of her employer, Edmund Mills, thereby putting him to a loss of 3s.—Ordered to pay damages and return to her work. SMASHING HER ROTHER'S WINDOW.—Sarah Robertson, of 56, Winwick-st., was charged with wilfully damaging the window of her brother, William Hollows, on Wednes- day night last. The prosecutor said that on the night in question, between 7 and 8, he heard a knock at the door, and on going to it, he found the defendant there. He asked her what she wanted there, and she commenced to shout. He did not want her there and he shut the door. As soon as he did so the stone (produced) came through his window. If it had come two or three inches further it would have broken the paraffin lampand set fire to the house.—The defendant said her mother told her that tne prosecutor had been to her house abusing her in most opprebious terms, and defaming her character. As he had done this several times she went to see him about it, and he so provoked her that she threw the stone through the window.—The prosecutor said hehad only used to his mother words repeated to him by the defendant herself. She was ordered to pay costs and damages together 7s 6d. CHARGE OF CRIMINAL ASSAULT.—John Jones, of 71, Catherine-st., wa;t charged with committing a rape on the night of the 22nd inst. or the morning of the 23rd on Sarah Ann Merryman' aged 15, daughter of Mrs. Merry- man, 35, Folly-lane. The complainant was in his employ as a servant, having been with him about six months. Mr. Browne appeared for the defence. He was coramitted for trial, bail being accepted—his own recognisances in £5O and two sureties in £25 each.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Marson (chairman), J. Crosfield, and Captain Withington. _ _ _ _ _ _
DRUNK.—John Millington,'drunk on S-aturday night, at renketh, was fined 6s. and costs.

THEFT OF A HANDKERCHIEF BY A BOY.—Joseph Barrow, aged 15, the son of respectable parents was charged with stealing, on the night of the 16th inst.' a silk handker- chief, value is. 2d., the property of Alfred Peacock, draper, from a stall in the Market Place, Earlestown. The prosecutor said a little after nine o'cleck on the night in question he noticed the prisoner in the company of another bey near the stall, and having the handkerchief in his hand, leaving the stall. Witness ran after him, but lost hina.—P.C. Boyes said he went to the prisoner's house on the night of the 16th inst., and appre- hended him. On being charged he replied "I am very sorry. I don't know what tempted me to take it." He handed witness the handkerchief. —Mr. Garland, ironmonger, of Warrington, said he was sorry to see the prisoner in such a position that morning. The lad was in his employ for two years,and until four months ago, at his place at Earlestown, and his manager reported to him that he always found him a very decent lad, and one that he trusted with anything. He had money passing through his hands day by day, and the mq.nager never found anything wrong:. The boy left to go to the Viaduct works where he could earn more money. It was only through the lad havintrgot into bad company that he had been led to commit this act, on the spur of the moment.— This being prisoner's first offence, the magistrates con- tented themselves with binding over his stepfather for A the lad's re-appearance if called upon at any future time, and requiring him to pay the costs.

The prisoner said he was poor and had no fire at home.—Superintendent Noblett informed the Bench that the prisoner had been three times convicted .of felony, on the Past ' occasion for stealing goods from a railway wagon.—Mr. Pilkington said considering the prisoner's previous character they could not do less than sentence htm to 3 days hard labour.

_ SLEEPING Our—Patrick McMahon, nt, fixed residence., was committed to goal for 14 days for sleeping in Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical works on Thurs6y morning.— Andrew McCann, a boy 13 years of age, residing with his parents in Pleasant-st., was charged with a like offence. ASSAULT.—Patrick Muldoo. n, 1, Brynn-st., Widnes,was summoued for assaulting Isabella Farnell, on the 19th inst. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. It appears that the complainant and her husband lodged with the defendant and on Monday morning, the complainant alleged that in her husband's absence the defendant assaulted her, and behaved in an indecent manner.—Mr. J. W. Knowles contended that the Bench could not convict the defend- ant, as there was no evidence of an assault having been committed.—The Bench held that the case had been proved, and fined the defendant 10s. and costs, or 14 days in default.
TOOMBALL--RUGPY.

The Rev. F. Marshail seems tT;-I;e7-d.etermined to re- open the Oldham business. He evidently thinks he has a case, and means to push it to the end. He loves to pose as the champion of amateurism, but can he not find sufficient occupation in his own shire? One would think there is at least as much room there for the "purity business "'as in Lancashire..

It is true that, the Coventry team, which was a pretty strong one; made the journey, but on the players viewing the ground they absolutely refused to turn out. The present season must have been a bad one for the finances of Rugby football club, and it is to be hoped that we have now seen the last of the frcst.
ANNUAL REPORT.

• In the annual report of the Council of the War- rington Chamber of Commerce, which will be pre- sented to the annual meeting to be held on Monday next, reference is made to the resolutions passed at the recent meeting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce, with regard to Boards of Arbitration in labour disputes, commercial education, &c. The report says :—" With reference to the question of Boards of Arbitration in labour disputes, it will be within the recollection of some of the members of the chamber, that such a bcdy was formed by the Warrington Cham- ber many years ago. Its services have, however, never been ,called into requisition. The scheme of commercial education of the London cliginber, has now been put into operation, and many of tde best comineicial houses (have pledged themselves to give the preference to appli- cants for employment holding the commercial certifi- cates. The Council forwarded a copy of the syllabus to the Warrington Teachers' Association, but the latter have as yet taken no action in the matter. The Council, act- ing in concert with the Corporation of Warrington,, and other interested authorities, recently approached the Manchester Ship Canal Company, with a view to inducing them to build the proposed bridge over the Mersey at Walton, at a higher level than that shown on the plans, as otherwise, owing to the low headway, communication with the docks from the river would have been cut off for boats of even very moderate size. There is every pro- spect of the bridge in question being built on the same level as the London and North-Western Railway Bridges, in which case the headway will be ample. Arrangements have been made with the Admiralty for the exhibition at the Chamber next spring, of samples of such heavy leather goods as they may require, so as to give greater facility to persons desiring to tender for their supply."
NEWTON-LE-W ILLOWS • CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual' general meeting of the members of the Newton-le-Willows Cricket and Bowling Club, was held at the Pied Bull Motel, on Monday even- ing. Mr. B. B. Glover, president of the club, pre- sided, and there were also present—Messrs.Brierley, Stuart, W. Longton, Liptrott, Bodmer, Barton, G. Clarke, H. J. Longton, Bateman, Hindley, Heaton, &c.

Tne financial statement showed the receipts, in- cluding a balance of £6 16s. Id. from 1889, to be £ll9 17s. 2d., and the expenditure £ll6 15s. id., leaving a balance of £3 2s. id. The accounts were adopted on the motion of Mr. R. Stuart, with the proviso, that the amount put down as receipts from Tennis Ball, be altered te " contribution " for Tennis Ball.
PATRONS.

Messrs. W. J. Leg!), T. W. Legh, M.P., and Colonel McCorquodale, were re-elected patrons .of the club.—On the motion of Mr. Clarke, seconded by Mr. Brierley, Mr. T. J. Gillespie's name was added to the list.,
ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.

Mr. R. Brierley, in proposing the re-election of Mr. B. B. Glover, said it gave him the sincerest pleasure to put before them the name of Mr. Glover, as he had filled the office in a manner that was most exemplary, and his recommendation needed no words of his (Mr. Brierley's). (Applause.)—Mr.Liptrott seconded, and the motion was unanimously adopted.—Mr. Glover said he was very much obliged to them for conferring the honour upon him for another year, but he had said they were making a mistake. They wanted fresh btoosi in the position of president; they wanted a man on the spot, who could be in touch with them weekly, and, in fact, daily, and he accepted the position on one or two conditions. He would accept it for the first twelve months, to see how it worked, and if at the end of that time it did not work, they could send each other about their businesses. (Ap- plause.)
TREASURER.

Mr. Glover proposed and Mr. Bodiner seconded that Mr. Barton be re-elected treasurer.—Mr. Barton said he came to that meeting purposely to resign the office. When he took the position of treasurer, he intended to become a bowling member, but since that time he had taken up other games,and he would rather not take office again.—Mr. Glover said if Mr. Barton could not take office as treasurer, he would suggest that they transfer him to the office Of vice-president, then they should have Mr. James Fairclough, Mr. Robert Stone, Mr. R. Brierley and Mr. Barton, and he would propose that.—Mr. Bod- mer seconded. Carried.—The Chairman then proposed that Mr. W. Hindley be treasurer, and Mr. Liptrott seconding, it was carried.
SEC RETAII I E S .
Mr: J. Liptrott proposed and Mr. R. Brierley seconded that Mr. Singleton be the bowling secretary, and Mr. Heaton the cricket secretary. Carried.
CAPTAINS.

On the motion of Mr. H. J. Longton, seconded by Mr. Bodmer, Mr. Hindley was appointed captain of the first leven, and Mr. Thomas Harrison was appointed captain of the second eleven, on the motion of Mr. T. Fairclough.—Mr. Stewart moved and Mr. Hibbert seconded, that the following be appointed captains of the bowling teams. Messrs. Bodmer, T. S..Fairclougli, J. Liptrott, and E. Fairclough, carried.—Mr. W. Longton was.appointed tennis captain, on the motion of Mr. J. Liptrott, seconded by Mr. Glover.

Sr. HELENS v. BLACIELEY.—St. Helens had a fixture with Blackley on Saturday, but it had to be abandoned on account of the hard state of the Blackley ground. WARRINGTON STAR 2ND v. RUNCORN JOCKEYS.—PIayed at Runcorn on Saturday last, and after a very hard fought game resulted in a win for the Star. Score--- Star, 1 try, 5 minors. Jockeys ISt, 1 minor. Anderton scored try.

LowroN V. WIDNIAS RANGRItS.—Lowton journeyed to Widnes on Saturday, when they met the Rangers of that town before a good number of spectators. The play was very even throughout, and ended Widnes Rangers 1 goal 1 minor, Lowton 1 try 1 minor. ST. ELPHIN'S• WADRINGTON V. ALTRINCHAM "A."—This match was played at Altrincham, on -Saturday, before a fair attendance. The visitors won the toss, and pressed during the first half, only minors being scored. Haimp- son re-started, and by good following up Daniels secured, and passing to Eden, that player had an easy journey over the line, but no goal resulted. Altrincliam roused themselves after this reverse, and forced a minor. The Saints again pressed on the drop out, and Cliffe got over, but the point was disallowed. Singleton scored imme- diately from a pass by Natton, the latter's kick at goal striking the upright. Time was now called, the final occrt)!ning St. Elphin's, 2 tries, 3 minors; Altrincham, 4. minors.

WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. STOCItTON FIEATK IST. The return match between these clubs took place on Saturday, on the ground of the former. The ground was in a hard condition but owing to the keen rivalry exist- ing between the teams, the game was played. Savage, on behalf of the Rangers, kicked off, play being evenly contested up to half time, Stockton Heath having advan- tage of 2 minors to nil. During the second half the home team had slightly the best of it, but both teams strove hard to obtain the verdict, and just on the call of time Fleming for the Rangers broke away and secured a clever try, which Potts converted into a goal. Final result :—Rangers, 1 goal 3 minors; Stockton Heath, 2 minors.

ST. HELENSRECREATION V. TYLDESLEY.—On Saturday afternoon fully six thousand spectators assembled on the Recreation ground to witness the match between St. Helens Recreation and Tyldesley. A large number of the spectators came from Tyldesley. The ground was covered during the week, and it was decided to play the proper game. It was expected that Mr. H. Seton-Karr, the borough member would be present to kick off, but he only made his 'appearance during the match, and he then walked round the field in company with Captain Thom- son. Shortly after the start, Hankinson picked up the ball and dropped it over the visitors' bar in splendid style, amid vociferous cheering. The subsequent play • was very fast and Hanson ran up to the line and grounded the ball, She.* landing a goal. This brought half-time with the score—Recs., one goal and two minors, Tyldesley, one goal and one minor. The only score in the second half was for the Recs. by Turton, who succeeded in grounding. Seddon failed to convert. The Recs. won a grand game by one goal, one try, and three minors to one goal and two minors.

CHESHIRE JUNIOR CUP. WESTON POINT. y. CHESTER ST. OSWALD'S.

While the prolonged frost has been giving the expo nents of Rugby football in Runcorn district a period of idleness, the local association club—Weston Point—has been gathering the laurels of fame, and a eorresponding increase of gate money. The Club is composed of employes on the Ship Canal at the village, and the field on which they have been doing doughty deeds is situated off Heath-road, Runcorn. During the season which is more than half finished, on only two occasions has the club retired vanquished, and as the principal junior clubs in the county and one or two on the Lancashire side have been met this is a fact that speaks well for their com- bination. At the present time they are engaged in an attempt to win-the Cheshire junior cup, and according to present appearance will have more than an ordinary "look in." A few weeks ago they met Chester St. John's in the first round, and threw them out by the score of three goals to nil. On Saturday afternoon they met another Chester club—the St. Oswald's—in the second round and the struggle was witnessed at Runcorn, by a couple of hundreds of spectators. Weston played with the slope of the ground in their favour the first half, but the game was, very equal for the first fifteen minutes. Both back divisions played a capital defensive game, and occasionally the forward ranks displayed some good passing tactics. At length after a combined run up. Blower sent the ball past Atherton amid loud cheers, and he had subse- quently to psi his hands several times to repel deter- mined attacks by the homesters. On changing ends, Chester scored in the first five minutes, Lloyd being responsible for the final shot, but this only caused Weston to play with more determinationiand their forwards now assumed the upper hands, and some very effective long passing took place. Garvey and Antrobus executed a pretty run on the left,and crossing opportunely Pye was enabled to put his side once more ahead. About ten minutes from time, A. Limb and Blower, rushed the ball up, and again Pye put the finishing touch, and at the call of time Weston had won by three goals, to Chester St. °maids one goal. The visitors were defeated on their merits. Throughout thegame they could not cope with the home back division, of whom Davies was a tower of strength in himself. The forwards all played a good combined game, and Blower deserves mention for a number of fine runs of the visitoie. Hughes was the pick. Their short passing proved far less effective than the long passing of the home team, The teams were as follows :—Weston: R. Limb, goal ; F. Davies, James Kidd, backs; James Limb, James Sproston, and John Limb, half-backs; A. Limb, W. Blower, 11. Pye (centre), Owen Garvey, and Isaac Antrobus, forwards.—Chester Atherton, goal; McNeil, and another, backs; Marsh, Palmer and Haymen, half-backs; Dodd, Roberts, Brown (centre), Lloyd and Hughes, forwards.
