div.head: AasocLLTioN.
div.p: AasocLLTioN.

That professionalism brings infinite trouble in its wake is made plain every day. Take the recent action of the Football Len gue,f or instance. Since open payment of players was legalised, they have east their nets in every coiner of the kingdom, with the result that every club of note has suffered more or less, and some have almost been reduced to a skeleton. And now what do we find? Why, that even though a man may desire a change of employment, clubs outside the &Ewe must riot make overtures to a League player without being boycotted. Ardwick have been seeking to strengthen their ranks on the same lines as the bigger organisations, and the fiat has gone forth that no League team must meet the Man- chester club. Everton can rob Dartven of their best player, but if Darwen Make an attempt to retaliate, they must be severely punished. Such selfishness as this is deplorable, and it must tend to destroy the pepularity of the League.

The Football Association Cup ties came out pretty much as was expected. Two League clubs that were supposed to have simple tasks before them only survived the round by the aid of extra time, these being Burnley and Wolv3rhampton Wanderers. Two others were knocked out of the competition, and in each instance previous form may be said to have been confirmed. The North End attack has been so weak and erratic that it was not surprising they should be beaten at Stoke. It was a surprise, however, that Stoke should score more goals against thein'than any team had done hitherto this season,—all the more credit to the victorious side. Sun- derland and Everton aro the best matched clubs in the kingdom. They have met each other three times, and victory has been repre,sent3d by a solitary goal in every instance. The luck of the draw gave the tie to Sunder- land, and Everton have already said farewell to the competition for another year. We would like to have seen them stay in it .much longer; but Fate has willed otherwise. They have still a good chance of the League honours.

Blackburn Rovers, Notts, Aston Villa, and Derby County are all ready for the next round, whilst among ether winners may be named Notts Forest, Darwen, and Sheffield Wednesday. The Forest figured as the heaviest goal-getters—N to none against Cla,pton,—and if they are anything like fortunate in the matter of the draw they may be regarded as dangerous customers. Accring- ton and the Bolton Wanderers will need to meet again, but the question of ground will have to be settled by the F. A. Council. There is not much to choose between the pair.

The attendance at some of the ties shows how keesnly the public follow the progress of the competition. At Sunderland there were 15,100 persons, at Sheffield (v. Notts) 10.000,at Middlesbrough (v. the Rovers) 12,000, at Stoke 8,000, and so on. It is worthy of note; too, that the 13 winners scored 68 goals to eight, that six of the beaterrteams failed to score at all, and six others had to rest satisfied with a goal apiece. Three of the victorious clubs ran into double figures, and two won by one point only.

The recent'clecisions of the Football League have, says a Blackburn correspondent, given rise to much dissatis- faction among the League clubs in Lancashire, and rumour is rife about the probability of a' split." Several prominent football officials are moving in the matter, and it is said that the whole of the Lancashire clubs —Everton, Blackburn Rovers; Preston North End, Burnley, Bolton Wanderers, Accrington together with Sunderland, will secede, and form a league of their own, to be called the Northern League. Should such a step be taken, it would be a serious matter for the Midland clubs, whose "gates" depend largely on the visits of the northern teams.

- The Rovers and North End are the only clubs that can beat the present number of points held by Everton, for Notts and WolverhaTnpton. can only reach 28 points, and Bolton Wanderers 27, so that all depends on the success of the Rovers and North End, and it is not likely that they are strong enough to win the whole of the matches they have to play.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

_ With regard to the contest last Friday evening between the teams of the Warrington and St. Helens gymnasium, we might very well use a stock phrase and say that St. Helens was defeated, but not disgraced. In fact the beaten team did remarkably well against such doughty opponents. The St. Helens me rt were altogether a slighter lot than the Warrington. They did not show anything like the physical development of their visitors, nor had they such a practised and confident way of going through their exercises.

It may be expected that before another twelve months elapse, the glass and chemical town will be able to bring together a very formidable team of athletes. They are certainly well favoured in one thing, and that is the possession of a fine gymnasium. In this respect they are at all events ahead of the Warringtonians.

There is now a good deal of speculation as to the posi- tion the Warrington team is likely to hold at the close of the competition for the challenge shield. They got up into the final last year, and this year it is hoped that they will not only get into the final, but secure at least second place when they are there. Of course they have stronzer teams than St. Helens to encounter, and it's never safe to prophesy unless you know.

div.head: FATAL EXPLOSION OF GUNPOWDER.
div.p: FATAL EXPLOSION OF GUNPOWDER.

A boy named Hunter, on Monday evening, took a lighted candle near a barrel of gunpowder, in the shop of Mr. Wm. Hunter, grocer, Dellshill, Lanarkshire, and the powder exploded, killing the boy, blowing down the shop, and seriously injuring four persons:

div.head: TWO MEN KILLED AT WHITBY.
div.p: TWO MEN KILLED AT WHITBY.

On Monday. while a number of men were engaged pulling down a massive wall at Whitby, a portion of the brickwork collapsed suddenly. Two of the workmen— James Pybus and %Villiani flebdon-were buried in the ruins and killed. Other .workmen had very narrow escapes.

div.head: SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE..
div.p: THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE..

The traffic on the Scotch railways was reported to be more satisfactork' on• Tuesday, though merchants are still complaining about the tardy transit of goods. The Edinburgh City Council and other public bodies have adopted memorials to the Board of Trade urging that the department should use its powers to ensure safe travell- ing and a better regulation of heavy traffic. The bulk of the men on strike remain unyielding, and there is no proffer of conciliation or concession from the directors. At the men's meeting on Tuesday at Edinburgh Mr. Tait said the railway servants were willing to consider any proposals the companies might make, but they weie anxious that the opinions of practical men should be taken on the matters in dispute. A telegram from Glas- gow states that forty-four Caledonian men, including nineteen drivers have offered themselves for re-engage- ment at Polmadei.

. _ On iVednesday most contradictory reports prevailed in Edinburgh and Glasgow with regard to the strike. The authorities alleged that there was a stanapedeof men anxious to return to work ' • but, on the other hand,, the strike executiveaskerted that of the forty-four men who went in at Polmadie on Tuesday trdenty-three had been recaptured, and ten English" blacklegs "had gone back home. The traffic returns issued on Wednesday show that so far,the strike has cost the three companies £ll2 793

It is reported that on the Caledonian and North British systems many additional hands have been engaged, and that the traffic is gradually improving. The men, on the other hand, assert that the new workers are of little use to the companies, and that there is yet a considerable block of goods and mineral traffic. From the mass meet- ing on Thursday in Edinburgh a telegram was sent to all the centres calling upon the men on strike to join in expressing their determination to yield to no 'influence whatever that would draw them back to railway service on intolerable terms. There seems to be little doubt, however, that some of the old servants are returhing to work.
Mr. Charles Thomas, of Bristol, has been appointed deputy chairman of the Midland Railway Company, in the place of Mr. George Ernest Paget, who recently became chairman.

Despatches received in Liverpool on Wednesday re- port a terrib:e tragedy at Ballarat, where a prominent business man named James Johnston smothered his four children as they lay in bed, and afterwards fatally shot his wife. He also turned the weapon on himself, and at latest accounts was lying in hospital. Official intelligenc,e from Chili on Tuesday is to the effect that the insurgent feet is blockading Valparaiso and Iquique, and that the diplomatic body of Santiago has protested against the blockade. A French cruiser will at once be despatched to Chilian waters.

div.head: COMMITERE,
div.p: COMMITERE,

The following were appointed to serve on the General Committee :—Messrs. Stuart, Bodmer, T. Brierly, G. Harrison, H. Hibbert, Parkes, Price, Latchford, Sankey, Sweetlove, Williamson, Berry, Wilkinson, and H. J. Longton.—Messrs. Wilkinson, F. Brierley, and F. San- key were selected as the Ground Committee.
LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE 130WLING ASSOCIATION

The Chairman said ,the next question was whether they should join the County Bowling Association.—Mr. Brierley said that before anything was done, he should be glad to have a report from Mr. Liptiott, as to their last years doings,—Mr. Liptrott said last year they suc- ceeded admirably,'and they might possibly win the cup again this year. Their position at the present time, how- 'ever, was not quite so satisfactory as it might be, but he did not think the present was the proper time to niention it. He thought a sub-committee should be appointed to see whether some means could not be devised for paying the ordinary expenses of those members who were selected to play in thecompetition. He should certainly advise them to join the Association, but he was not prepared with any suggestion at the present time, as to what course he should take.—The Chairman thought they should certainly join the Association, as he thought the Newton players had improved very much by corning in, contact with other clubs, and the tone of the whole thing was raised. He should propose that they raise the tone still higher. When first these county matches were played, he beard a certain amount of betting going on, but last year, he heard nothing of the sort, and the game was played with a thorough 'genial spirit on both sides. Mr. Liptrott's point was really one of detail, which they could fight out in committee, but he did not think it was fair for the junior members of the dub to contribute one single penny towards the expenses of those who played in the county matches.—Mr. Barton said it was opening a very wide question, as when the cricketers go from home they pay their own expeuses,and it was quite unnecessrry to pay the expenses of the bowlers from the club funds.—Mr. Stuart then moved that they join the County Association, and remarked that he did not think the players in the cup competition should have their ex- penses paid ; he thought it was quite honour enough for lhem to have their names inscribed on the cap.—Mr. Liptrott said he did not say that they wanted the club to pay the bowlers' expenses, but they wanted some means devising by which the best men could be selected.--Mr. Brierley seconded the proposition and it was carried.

div.head: PROFESSIONAL.
div.p: PROFESSIONAL.

Mr. Glover said they had been making a mistake for a long time, by not having a professional to coach young players, and the sooner they could expend a little extra money upon a professional, who would be on the ground to coach the young players, the better it would be. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Stuart thought it was worth the efforts of the club to endeavour to get a professional, and he would move that they get one.—,Mr. H. .r. Longton was quite in sympathy with what had been said as to the disirability of improving the club, but he had always ooine to the conclusion that finances had a groat deal ot do with the prosperity of the club. His opinion was that they could not afford a professional and for that reason he should oppose it.—The Chairman said it was not a question of expense, but simply one of re-arranging the finances. They could well afford to pay a professional if they made up their minds, and it was his opinion that it would pay them to get one this year.—Mr. J. Brierley seconded Mr. Stuart's Motion.—Mr. Liptroth said if he could see his way to find the means by which they could afford to pay for a professional, he should be pleased to vote for one. If they wanted s professional cricketer they must have a groundsman a. well. It was utterly impossible to get a professional and groundsman in one. He concluded by seconding M , Longton's amendment.—Mr. Barton said their finances would stand a professional. He agreed with Mr. Glover,. and Mr. Stuart, that if they had not a professional they would only be a second-rate club. Ho thought they would make a great mistake, if they did not have a pro- fessional for this year.—Mr. Hindley said it was too late now to obtain a good professional, as they were all en- gaged. July Or August was the best time to apply for them.—Mr. Briefly- thought there was no harm in trying to get one.—A;ter. some further discussion a vote was taken, and Mr. Longton's amendment was carried.

div.head: AUDITORS.
div.p: AUDITORS.
Messrs. T. S. FairclouWa-n-d—Zooke jun., were elected auditors.
LAWN TENNIS CLUB.

A long and heated discussion took place in connection with the above, as to the amount of subscription mem- bers wishing to join it should pay. Ultimately a motion by Mr. Barton and seconded by Mr. Longton,that gentle- men should pay five shillings over and above their ordin- ary cricket subscription, apd ladies five shillings also, was carried.
OPENING DAY.
This question was left for the decision of the Com- mittee. This being all the business, the meeting closed with a vote of thauks to the Chairman.

div.p: MR. SETON KA.RR M.P., AT ST. HELENS.
In addition to the initiation of Mr. H. Seton Barr, M.P., as a member ea St. Helens Lodge of Odd- fellows, reported in another column, he again visited the constituency on Monday.

div.head: DEPUTATIONS.
div.p: DEPUTATIONS.

At noon a deputation from the steam engine and boiler minders waited upon him at the Conservative Club, Hall-st. The deputation consisted of Coun- cillor Robert Hunter and Mr. F. Eden, and there was a long conversation with regard to the prospects of the Bill for making it compulsory upon all men having charge of steam engines and boilers to undergo an examination, and to be granted certifi- cates of competency. Mr. Seton Karr, M.P., has introduced the measurein the House of Commons, and it is down for second reading on the 10th proximo. Mr. Seton Karr promised the deputation that he should do his utmost to get the Bill brought forward on the day in question, and if lie was unsucccessful he should do his utmost to get it before- the House at the earliest possible moment. It is stated that nume- rous petitions in support of the Bill are being signed by the working-classes of St. Helens, particularly those in- terested in engines and Machinery. On Monday after- noon Mr. Thomas Glover, the miners' agent, also waited upon Mr. Seton-Karr at the club. In the course of conversation upon mining questions generally, Mr. Seton-Karr stated that he was in favour of the proposed Eight Hours Bill for Miculrs, and should vote in its sup- port when it was brought forward in the House of Com- mons. In regard to the Employers' Liability Bill audits proposed compulsory clauses, Mr. Seton-Karr said he could support the proposals to some extent, but before coming to a final decision,he required time for considera- tion of the question in all its bearings.
POLITICAL SPEECH.

On Monday night, Mr. Seton Karr, M.P. , attended a miscellaneous concert in aid of the funds of the Conser- vative and Unionist Working Men's Association held in the assembly room, of the Conservative Club. Councillor W. J. Thomason presided, and among those present were Major M‘Tear C.ounoillors Massey and Morgan, Messrs. C. Culshaw, H. S. Oppenheim, J. 0. Swift, T. Crooks, Seton Karr, in the course of an address, said he thought the present Government had a very fair record of its performance during its reign. Their foreign policy had been above suspicion, and could not even be blamed by their' opponent& Their domestic policy was of a somewhat similar character. They had passed measures for the benefit of working-men both in town and country, they had saved the national money, reduced the national debt, strengthened the national defences, and reduced taxation. With regard to their Irish policy, they had not only maintained law and prder, but had increased the material pros- perity of the country. The Home Rule policy of Mr. Gladstone was shattered into fragments, and he thought they were justified in saying that their opponents were absolutely without a policy. They were politically naked, and, if he might use an ancient simile, they were as naked as were our first parents in the .Garden of Eden ; but there was this difference, that our first parents had a morality above suspicion ; the politi- cal morality of the Gladstonian party was at present beneath contempt. (Applause.) There was no half-way between Home Rule and total separation. There was only one thing which would satisfy the Irish party, and that was total separation. Every week that passed by strengthened the cause of the Unionists on the one hand, and on the other the Uladstonian party sank deeper and deeper into the mire. They had only to be given rope enough and they and their Irish allies would sooner or later be sure to hang themselves if they had not already done so. (Applause.)—A cordial vote of thanks was tendered to Mr. Seton-Karr, M. P., for his address, and the Concert was resumed. LECTURE ON " WEALTH AND POVERTY." _

_ On Tuesday night Mr. H. eton-Karr, M.P., gave a lecture on" Wealth and Poverty," in the gymnasium of the Young Men's Christian Association. There was a good attendance, and Councillor H. Martin presided. Among those present were Major Windus, Major M'Tear, Councillor Massey, Messrs. Joseph Robinson, B. H. Lomax, &.-.c.—Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., who was warmly received, contrasted the vast wealth possessed by some classes with the poverty and wretchedness existing in many quarters of the kingdom, and said to his mind there were three auses which had brought about the "inequality in the distribution of wealth. The first was the concentration of land in few hands; the second the enormous increase in commercial wealth and commer- cial enterprise during the last 30 or 40 years; and the third was the rise of the political economist. The in- equality in the distribution of wealth brought about poverty and crime, and necessitated our poor laws, our workhouse, our police, our law courts and judges, and our prisons, and was the great source of constantly re- curring labour struggles. Proceeding to deal with sug- gested remedies he considered that arbitration would do very much in that direction,and urged that unless capital and labour could amicably work together the only result would be injury to both. He did not agree with the swested nationalisation of land, but temperance legis- lation might do something towards mitigating the evils arising`from the drink traffic. The remedy for poverty suggested by General Booth might do much, but he did

A meeting of the West Derby Liberal Association l'?afi held on Monday night, in Derby Hall, Baker- Liverpool, under the auspices of the Liverpool Liberal Federal Council. Mr. W. To his t-rlind that struggle, and the outcome of it, showed that a,„ Ili. eh were as fit for Home Rule, if not more so, than 1 'Y In Lancashire or Cheshire. When had they in Eng- trd had such temptation put before them—a man whom ~,er had venerated half a life-time falling away from the ;tea of virtue ? It is in the neighbourhood of" • ." Seville, that the oramges best suited for " J-11 marmalade making are grevrn. A recent" "'lost (the like of wh'cli has not been ex-" " .perienced for ten years), has played havoc" "with the fruit, and, although though the" t' full extent of the damage is not yet" ' known, it is believed that fully one half " "the orange crop has been destroyed." "Luckily one shipment has been made to" "Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" "SS " Zurbumn," which has just arrived." " The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett." "Limited, haw, been fgrtunatc enough to" "have a large consignment on Board this" "vessel, but they do not anticipate getting "nearly sufficient to meet the demand for" "their well known marmalade, the sale of" "which is fast increasing."

OUR JUNIORS' CLUBS.

Sir,—l hope you wiil allow me a little space in your valuable paper as regards the Juniors' Clubs of War- rington. I see in the sporting issue of the Liverpool "Echo," on Saturday last, that the Widnes R.F.C. are giowu to play twenty of the junior players of Widnes, the proceeds to b.e Cii`ncitA Itriletl4.s tbc four clubs, from 4141014 the twenty pliyers are picked. Could not a com- mittee of the Juniors' Clubs be formed in Warrington, and send a deputation to the committee of the Warring- ton R.F.C. to follow the example of the Widnes F.C., and arrange a match to be played on the ground of the W.F.C. after the Warrington F.C. season is up, under this Leading—Warrington v. 20 Juniors of the town ? It would encourage our few Juniors' Clubs a little. The teams could be chosen from the four following clubs, viz. :—St. Elphin's, Rangers. Stars, and Stockton Heath F.C. There are three reasons why the Warrington club should consent to this—lst, because they are a club ef better standing than Widnes P.C.; 2nd, because, taken on an average, they get twice as many spectators; 3rd, because, the. past Juniors' Club of the town has helped to bring the W.F.C. to the proud position they now hold. Hoping that some mightier pen will take this up,. and the Junior Committee will be formed as quickly as pos- sible, I remain yours very truly, Warrington, January 19th, 1891.
GRAND STAND.

div.head: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

Sir,—From the report of the proceedings of the last meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners which appea,rta in your valuable paper of the 3rd inst., I observe that:the Local Government Board have de- clined to san4ipn, a gratuity of £5O to the Law Clerk for extra and that the Commissioners, not to be frustrated in their desire to reward him for doing no more than his duty, propose in lieu thereof to increase his salary by £25 per annum, notwithstanding that they fixed a maximum sum for the duties of his office only about two years ago. The Board, I believe, took much time to deliberate on this matter, and mado various in- quiries before coming to a deeision in order that they might agree upon an amount which would be fair to all parties. True, he has had a little extra work, and all offices are subject to this, but there has been no perma- nent increase in the duties, which are practically the same now as when he undertook them. I should like, therefore, to ask wherein is the utility of making such an arrangement as the one referred to if it is to be upset so soon after it has been made? The 'alteration in the method of remuneration will no doubt be appre- ciated by the recipient, though not so pleasing to the ratepayers who will be charged with £25 annually instead of £5O down, unless the resolution to increase the stipend is to be rescinded immediately what is called the "just obligation" is discharged. While drawing attention to this matter, I think it would not be out of place to enumerate, for the informa- tion of the ratepayers, the amount of salaries paid by the Board during the past six years. They are as follows Year ending 25th March
Amount of salaries 2 g. d. 1885 1836 1887 1888 1889 1890

Comment is needless, the figuresspeak for themselves, but one thing is certain that their expansion is out of all Droportion to the growth of the town. The payments for 1890 represent no less than fourpence in the pound on the assessable value, according to the General District Rate. During 1889 the place made a retrograde move- ment, the assessable value for that year being less than in the previous one.—Yours truly. QLTI VIVE.
Runcorn, 13th January, 1890.
IGNORANCE AS AN AID TO FAITH.
"Where ignorance is bliss 'tis.fouv to be wise.,,

Sir,—Certain of your correspondents have of late been committing the grave and unpardonable fault of asking people to think upon matters outside the constricted routine of their daily lives; to think for themselves on matters religious, and to examine the basis upon which their own faith is fixed. As one of the sirmers in this respect I have come to ask myself—why should we ask these good folk to undergo the, to them, unaccustomed agonies of connected cogitation ? To place before the mind of the average Christian as he plods among the petty details of ordinary life, the pons asinoruna of ab- stract thought is tantamount to the infliction of an injury if not an insult. They naturally object. to being dragged from the Sleepy Hollow of their own little sec- tarianism, in the drowsy atmosphere of which they doze away their time under the pleasing delusion that they are Christians. They inherit their faith with their sur- names, as something for which their fathers and not themselves are responsible. Although they would be ashamed to wear the antiquated suits of their ancestors, they do not scorn to clothe their minds in the worn out and unmendable mental habiliments of byegone genera- ' tions. But, as a palliation, if not an entire excuse, for our offence, I would offer the plea that it was done with the best intention—the desire to advance the truth. Now many, if not most, of the good people whom we have been tempting to tread the thorny paths of polemical discussion, annually transport their bodies to the seaside

TOLSTOI AND CHRISTIANITY,

Sir,—Mr. Dignum says he feels compelled to correct the very inaccurate statements I have made respecting Mr. Beet's words in the" Credentials of Religion." I did net profess to quote Mr. Beet's words. I gave what I conceived to be the only construction that can be put upon his words. Now Mr. Dignum gives us his exact words, and I ask, can any -other construction be put upon them than the one I gave? Will your readers fol- low closely what Mr. Beet really says: "We have nothing from the pen of Christ. The first five books of the new Testament are anonymous. For the names commonly attached to the four Gospels, although found in our earliest copies are doubtless of later date, and do but embody a; very ancient tradition." Now I contend that these words bear the interpretation I put upon them. Certain names are attached to the four Gospels: either these names are those of the authors or they are not. If they are the names of the authors, then they are not anonymous, but, if Mr. Beet's statement that they are anonymous is correct, then it follows that their authorship is involved in great doubt; it follows that we have no certainty that they were written by their reputed authors. If the names commonly attached to them "do but embody a very ancient tradition," then I think lam justified in saying that, according to Mr. , Beet, no one knows when, or where, or by whom, they I were written.

Mr. Dignum says that a book may be anonymous, though it may be well-known who wrote It. This is quite true, but how does it apply in the present : case? Turning to the dictionary, I find the word anonymous defined as, "having no name attached, without the name of the author." But hero we have the names attached: we have the names 1 Mathew' Mark, Luke, and John. Then how can the books be anonymous? Me. Beet can only mean that we have no certainty that they were written by their reputed authors; that, in fact, the names I attached to them "do but embody a very ancient tradi- tion." This is proved by Mr. Beet's very next passage. He says, "We therefore pass over these books for the moment, in favour of thirteen letters which bear the name of the Apostle Paul, and thus make a definite claim touching their authorship. All these were accepted throughout the Roman Empire with perfeet confidence as the genuine works of the great apostle." Who can doubt for a momeat after reading these words that Mr. Beet claims for the Epistles that they were genuine—that they were really written by St. Paul whose name they bore—but that he cannot claim as much for the Gospels, as they are anonymous—as the names attached to them "do but embody a very ancient tradition." I hope your readers will clearly understand me. It is not I, but Mr. Beet, who says that the Gospels are anonymous. I have own opinion—but lam dealing now with Mr. Beet's opinions. . . .

'Now as to the disciples misunderstanding Christ, nay friend reminds me of the promise of Christ to His disciples that the Father would send His Spirit to teach them all things, and that the Spirit was bestowed upon them at Pentecost. Well, the account of Pentecost is given in the" Acts of the Apostles," and Mr. Beet says that the "Acts of the Apostles" is anonymous so that we have to depend upon an- unknown writer anonymous, a very impro- bable story. Any claim that Mr. Beet or Mr. Dignum may make on behalf of St. Paul,or the other Apostles,of being specially inspired by God falls utterly to the ground , when we find these apostles preaching such doctrines as the Fall and the Redemption which are so utterly opposed to the teaching of Christ. As Mr. Dignum is aware, I once believed these dogmas. But my belief was merely an unreasoning assent. I believed them because I had from my infancy been taught them. It was only when , I began to think for myself, instead of letting others think ,for me, that I realized how absolutely false and pernicious they were. As to the Fall,science gives it the lie direct, and history tells us that the further back we trace the story cf man, the less civilised and the more barbarous he was. But independently of either science or history, let any man look into his own breast and ask himself if such a story can by any possibility be true ? We are told that God created man in his own image and placed him in the garden of Eden. 'This garden has always been depicted las something gloriously beautiful. Poets and divines unnumbered have dwelt in rapturous strains on its sur- passing loveliness. And this paradise was given to man that he might be happy therein. One condition only was enacted. He was not to eat of the fruit of one tree. Now, we are told that God knows everything—that He knows beforehand everything that will happen. If this be true, then He know before He made this condition with Adam that he, poor Adam, would never be able to keep it. lie knew that the weakness of Adam's nature when assailed by the sophisms and blandishments of the serpent would prove too much for him. Then why mock Adam with II such a condition? And then to curse him, and for do- ing such a trifling thing ! Would any father deserving the name deliberately put a temptation in the way of his child—knowing full well that the child would not be able to resist the temptation ? Would lie not rather have removed one supposing one to have been already in its way? And can any one conceive God doing such a thing? The idea is revolting to me. I turn now to Mr. Peers. I imam no objection to dis- cuss the Bible with him at seine future tune, but I must remind him that for the present the point at issue is "Can Tolstoi be a Christian and yet reject the dogmas of the Fall and the Redemption ?" I say he can. I say that not only does Christ not teach these dogmas,but that he does not even mention them. I say further that his teachings are utterly opposed to them. He teaches the love and the Fatherhood of God; and if God is the father of men and loves His children He could never have put a temptation in their way. He could never have mocked them with an impossible condition of happiness. He could never have cursed them for a trifling act of dis- obedience; and He'could never have required the shed- ding of innocent blood before He could forgive His poor sinful creatures, the work of His own hands, made after His own image, and who, in spite of all their deplorable wickedness, are yet the noblest and most god-like of all His creatures. But orthodox Christianity goes be:7(lnd even this and thinks it extols the glory and majesty of God by raving about

"A dreadful Hell. With never ending flames, Where sinners will with devils dwell, Bound in eternal chains." Better deny God altogether than dishonour -Him with such drivel as this. I again commend the careful and thoughtful reading of the works of Mr. Beet, Dr. Daßinger, F. Ballard, and others. But I don't anticipate the same results as Mr. Dignum. In my owncase they certainly opened my eyes, but not as my friend desired.—Yours truly, JOHN GANDY.

SIR WILLIAM GULL.

Tkodeath of Sir William Gull, which took ,place' MI the 29th January last, was a great loss to the medical profession in Eng- Tri , . Iv' ' ! ' IP--.d. He was born ix 1816, 146,q, " . i d, like many men who had '! V ..--„, en to 'eminence, he was of e-..,. ...tk -I-- 4r::,-. • • ''' •.7:7/1 1,. '4,-... •) , mble origin, his father ]iv at Thorpe-le-,Soken, Essex. was educated privately, \ subsequently pursued his ies at Guy's Hospital. He duated M. 8., in 1841, and .D. in 1846, at the London Ur' • ; and it is-.,worthy Of note that he was the' first medical graduate who was nominated on the Senate by the Crown. His first groat step in practice was in connection with the last illness of Bishop Blosifield in 1857, and after this he rapidly rose in the estimation of the public until the time when, as Physician-in-Ordinary to the Prince of Wales, he took the chief direction of the treatment of his Royal Highness during his attack of typhoid fever at the close of 1871. In acknowledgement of his services on that occasion he was created a baro- net in January, 1827, and Physician Extraordinary to the Queen, and was made Physician-in-Ordinary in 1887. In 1883 he resigned the position which he had held for twelve years in the General Medical Council as one of the Crown members. Sir William Gull was in his time president of the Clinical Society, a Fellow of the Royals Medico-Chirurgical Society, a member of tbe General Medical Council, an honorary Doctor of aril Law of Oxford, and a Fellow of the Royal Society. He was the author of several writings On medical subjecte., including treatises on " Hypochondriasis," and on "Abscess of the Brain," "Report on Epidemic Cholera, drawn r.p at the desire of the Cholera Committee of the Royal College of Physicians" (in conjunction with Dr. William Baly), 1854; "An oration delivered before the Hunterian Society, February 13th, 1861;" "Clinical observation in Relation to Medicine in Modern Times," an address delivered in the Divinity School, Oxford, on the occasion of the meeting of the British Association in that city in 1868; and "The Harveian Oration, delivered at the Royal Col- lege of Physicians, London, June 24th' 1810," The litter Work led to the publication of "The Mystery of Life ; an essay in re-ply to Dr. Gull's attack en the Theory of Vitality, in his llarveian Oration for 1870." By Lionel S. Beale, M. 8., F.R.S. Sir William Gull was also a frequent contributor to the reports of Guy's hospital. His speciality lay in clinical practice. He married in 1848 Susan Anne, daughter of Colouci J. Dacre Lacy, of Carlisle.
MR JAMES NASMYTH.
The. inventer of the steam hammer, Mr. James Nasmyth, died on the,7th May last, at the ripe age

of 81 years. He was. the son of a well-known landscape • painter, and was born in Edin- , burgh, on August 19, 1808. In his earliest days he gave evi- dence of a decided taste for •,="-v • mechanical pursuits; and in- -. eed he so readily acquired , he art of handling tools and ' donning the processes in actical mechanics that 'he to pay the fees for his attendance at the chemistry, mathematical, and natural philo- sophy classes at the Edinhurgh University, from the proceeds of the sale of steam-engine and other models which he constructed in a small workroom in his father's house... He commenced business in Manchester in 1834. The original workshops soon became too small for the business that came to him, and Mr. Nasmyth then removed to a twelve acre plot which he secured at ratricroft. This site was soon covered with an extensive series of workshops, and the establishment was named the Bridgewater Foundry, from the circumstance that the land was bounded by the Bridgewater canal. Here many mechanical tools were invented and manufactured which are now doing good service in the workshops of the world. Conspicuous among them is the steam hammer, which, since its invention in 1839 has had no small influence in advancing the progress of the mechanical arts. Among other inventions of his which have been extensively adopted owing to their high practical utility, may be mentioned the safety foundry, ladle, by whien the most ponderous casting can be poured with perfect security to the workmen; a suction fan,for effecting the perfect ven- tilation of mines,; a reversible rolling mill in which all,need of a fly wheel is dispensed with; a form of steam engine derived from that of his steam ham- mer, and largely adopted for screw steam-ships; and a spherical seated safety valve, which is abso- lutely perfect in its action. Having realised an ample fortune, he retired in 1857 from the firm of Masmyt'n, Gaskell, & Co., and from that time till his death he resided in Kent, engaging his time in pursuits of ti scientific character.

div.head: BY SPECTATOR.
div.p: BY SPECTATOR.

My " green and salad" days being o'er, I am not much given to rambling about the country, either in search of the beautiful or in pursuit of the"sweet Science" of botany. The chief lines of beauty to come within my view are the tountless chimneys of Widnes, and, as for the spirit of investigation, I am given sufficient employment in that direction in attempting to give a name (their habitation is an too apparent) to the varied smells that assail my nostrils almost daily, without . -entering upon a microscropic examination of rose lgaves. But the other day, filled with a desire to see how the great scheme of the Ship Canal, which is to • make Run- corn a city sometime in the future, was progress- ing in the neighbourhood, I went farther abroad than usual. As I only intended to tro-ti over the Runcorn &Wiwi, I made a start for Weeton Point, and sauntered by way of what is commonly known as "Cock and Hen-lane," but which is more politely called " Love-lane by the numerous young men and maidens, who make it their promenade., when the trees-are filled with foliage and the meadows smile with plenty. And a very appropriate name too. The warning notice" beware of the dogs." a prominent feature of Crofton Lodge, the residence of a locat magistrate, caused me to hurry past. as I have no great affection for the friend of man." when. he is a stranger; and I quickly ar- rived at the Salt Works, where trade is stagnant becanse the adjaining canal is bound by the icy monarch, and the boatman's hoarse cry of" gee up' is hushed. Considering the amount of steam aris- ing from the works. I should imagine that salt boil- ing was preceeding. While taking a look round, a Man deposited a large barrowful of hot clinkerA close by, and there was immediately a scramble by about a d9fen lads to fill the bags and basket's of very description and size Nithieli they carried. The pinch of the "laird times was evidently being felt at home. but how they were going to make a fire of the hard earthly natureless lftiiipt was a puzzle to me, and it was no nearer- solution wlien a few yards further:l came across a large hut.,-.id uliotantial ;it lotiked--:niade of bititilar 'clinkers. nowever, on wa,tked.and was soon • - - : :

TII• POINT .!which was as !quiet and sleepy as any port well Could be. In fact ut for the unloading of the steamer "Cecil," charfeted- With - Ship Canal 'materials, there appeared no trade doing whatever: the port was practically eiiiPry".-'lVbfk 'Was- how- I ever proceeding at the smithy and joiner's shop, of the ship Canal contractor, and there was a clang of . the hammers and the whirr of the saws to be heard. Walking on past the navvies' houses, I came across a large number of huge blocks of Welsh limestone ' some of which were only half-dressed, the masons having evidently been driven away by king frost. To fulfil the mission on which I had pet out, a walk along the railway, which ,runs on piles into the river about a quarter of a mile to the Weaver sluices, was necessary, and it was not altogether pleasant, this slippery weather, walking on 'planks 25 feet above the river bed, with the added • discomfort. of: dodging a locomotive occasionally. However I safely arrived opposite the sluices vfilich are a magnificent piece of work. Ten in number ther are built of 'the' best bricks faced -with blocks 414 local red sandstone to a height of 44 feet, and restV ing upon the solid foundation of concrete, laid deep.,' down in the bed of the river. Between these im mense walls of masonry huge iron gates are. placed, which can be raised and lowered at will. by.meiiis of hydraulic pressure.' These sluices will ferna part of the outer wall of the .canal, at.this point will divide the estuary of the Weaver from the Mersey and they' are constructed for the pur- poSe-of allowing the watersot the Mersey to flow in and out ot the Weaver when the tide is flowing. The estuary will form one lake of vast proportions through which the steamers and other ships will pass on their way to and from Manchester. At the present time a bank of soil is being deposited from Frodsham Marsh to the sluices, and it will then be necessary to work them daily. The gearing is already in trial. -Nearly a mile higher up the Weaver,! ,

div.head: MARSH LOCK
div.p: THE MARSH LOCK

is approaching completion. It is of dimensions capable of accommodating the largest vessels likely to steam up the catral. By means of gates, how- ever. it can be convertad into four locks, so that small craft can be transferred to the Weaver canal without a useless expenclitute of water and power. Three of these gates are already hung, and the stone work is progressing at a favourable rate. This lock has been in course of construction about two years, and when completed will be a monument to the ability of the agent, Mr. Y. Weston. Returning to Runcorn along the shores of the Mersey, I find that in the river opposite the Pumping Engine, pre- parations are being made for constructing the Bridgewater Lock, through which it is intended that vessels for Runcorn Docks shall pass from here ' river through the canal to the Docks. A pile driver is busily at work driving piles for the construction of the dams necessary to exclude the water and lay the foundations. A long line of piles from here stretches up to past the entrance to the tidal basin, on to the lower end of No Man's Land. Vessels and flats have now therefore to navigate a channel to reach the docks, which will ultimately be the canal proper ; and unfortunately at the entrance to this channel or passage,or by whatever name it is called,

div.head: LARGE SANDBANK HAS FORMED.
div.p: A LARGE SANDBANK HAS FORMED.

It is a great hindrance to navigation, and is giving great concern to all interestei. The Mersey has always been celebrated for its enormous shifting sandbanks,and whether this is, a " natural " silting up in consequence of the Ship Canal operations I must leave to experts to decide. Its presence is only too evident, and the difficulty and danger it causes are said to be seriously affecting the trade of the port. I was told that during a recent neap tide a flat drawing only five feet of water grounded on this small edition of Liverpool's bane, the Pluckington Bank. Captains of schooners will not, if they can possibly avoid it, charter their vegsels for Runcorn, and as the shipping trade is a.most important part of the industry of Runcorn this is a very serious matter. When I paid my . visit, the absence of ships from the docks was very conspicuous. Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, has inspected the bank, and as the ship Canal Company are deeply interested in the prosperity of the port, they will no doubt use every possible effort to clear away the obstruction, and for t le sake of the town it is to be hoped they will suoceed. The seal of the Board of Commissioners i is a ship n full sail, and it would be a thousand pities if they had to substitute one dis- playing a broken-backed schooner stranded on a mud bank, though this would only be a small matter compared with the loss to thetradesmen should the entrance to the port continue impeded. At Runcorn Bridge I found the work of constructing the con- crete wall of the Canal proceeding steadily. The wall stretches out a foot or two near Old Quay daily, and there is quite a long length now com- pleted. " Little drops of water, little grains of sand," are making, not a mighty ocean, but a wall for the Ship Canal which, if appearance goes for anything, will last all time.

div.head: AT OLD QUAY
div.p: AT OLD QUAY

Greater activity is displayed than has been the case for months past. I start is being made with the lock, which is to admit into the canal the craft from Widnes. Two pile drivers, with measured beat and slow, are driving into the bed of the river i huge beams of wood, n order to make a dam in which to place the foundations. Another machine of the some description is also driving piles, in which a "gantry is to run between Old Quay and No Man's Land. Turning inland, a walk to the Big Field at Norton showed that things were very quiet, the chief work in hand being the forming of the canal by means of two steam navvies, and as at some points a depth of over 60 feet has to be ex- cavated, before the level of the bottom of the canal is reached there is employment for them for some time to come. In fact the deepest cutting between Manchester and Eastham occurs.at Old Quay, op- posite the chemical works of Wigg, Bros., & Steele. i I learned that n future Mr. Weston would have the oversight of both the Weston and Runcorn sec- tions, and that the office and staff at Big Field would be dispensed with entirely, the chief office being located at No Man's Land, in Runcorn. To what use the fine offices constructed by Mr. Thomas Kirkham, at Big Field, will be put, I was unable to ascertain. Such are the items I was enabled to gather during my little.tramp ; and expressing the hope that they may interest. the readers of the "Examiner," I put my feet into my slippers and settle down for a rest and a smoke.

div.head: SFVERE WEATHER.
div.p: THE SFVERE WEATHER.
SKATING AT WARRINGTON.

Skating has bees very largely indulged in at Warrington during the last few weeks, and those who take part in this healthful pastime have been peculiarly favoured by the fine stretch of ice on the river diversion at Arpley. The cutting is about three quarters of a mile in length and of consider- able width and. it was covered with a thick sheet of ice over its whole course. It was estimated that on Sunday afternoon there were nearly 3,000 per- -lie on the ice, and an equal number of spectators on the banks. In addition to the skaters there were two or three young men on the ice on bicycles. On Monday there were again many skaters at Arpley, but in the evening, a thaw set in, and on Tuesday the Ship Canal authorities thought it desirable to bleak up the ice with explosives in order to pre- vent anctdents.

On the Ship Canal cutting from Morris Brook to Rixton, where the water has not been pumped out since the last flood, the ice was found -ta be in a splendid condition and attracted a large number of spectaters both on Saturday and Sunday.

div.head: LYMf.
div.p: LYMf.

There was a large number of visitors to Lymm on Saturday, for the purpose of 'skating on the dam. The ice was very good, that on the upper dam being the best, and as the scenery all around is very pretty the skaters had altogether a pleasant ti me of-it.

On Wednesday evening, in connection with the Mutual Improvement Association, Mi. J. Peers gave a lecture on" Time,how it is obtained and how kept." The paper was given in a most effecrive manner, and attentively listened to by the members. We purpose giving an abstract of it in our next issue.

PENNY BANE. Recently at a meeting in the Wesleyan Day School, Mr. Garnett called attention to the position, of the Penketh Penny Bank. Dnring the past year 53 new accounts have been opened, 1,608 transac- tions have taken place, £322 103. 3d. has been de- posited during this period, and £146 Ds. 4d. has been withdrawn. There was at the end of December the sum of £1,146 Ws. Ild, invested in the savings bank, debentures, and in the treasurer's hands. Interest at the rate of three per cent. is allowed on all sums amounting to 208.

div.head: WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.
div.p: WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.

A public entertainment in connection with the above was given, on Thursday afternoon, in the schoolroom. The chair will occupied by Mr. C. E. Parker, and there was a good attendance of parents and friends. An excellent programme consisting of songs, glees, readings and recitations was eantri- buted by the elder members and friends of the society, in a manner which was greatly appreciated by the audience. At the end of the programme, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Parker for his services in the chair fold also to the friends who had provided the evening's entertainment. A collec- tion was taken at the door in aid of the funds of the society.
CADISREAD.

TEXPERANCE MEETING.—A public metting was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, .on Saturday . evening. A special temperance address was given by Mr. G. Whit- field. Mr. Thomas Yates gave a reading entitled "The Adventures of a Monkey," which was well received. Mr. Worthington was in the chair. THE POST OFFICE.—Last week the Cadishead Post Office was removed to more commodious premises from the centre of the village. To meet the urgent requirements of the central population, a box has been placed near the Coach and Horses; which will partially reconcile the in- habitants to the change. OLD FOLKS' PARTY.—On Monday evening an old folks' party was held in the Ship Canal Mission Hall. The party was brought together by the ministers of the vari- ous denominations in the village. Two hundred sat down to an excellent tea. At the entertainment which followed the public vere admitted at a small charge. A capital programme had been provided. The chairman was Dr. E. 0. Jago, and the accompanist Mr. N. F. Clegg. At the close each woman received half-a-peutul of tea, while the men received an ounce of tobacco.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

CONGREGATIONAL TiA MEETING.—The Congregationa- lists held their annual social tea in the schoolroom on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance at the tea, and afterwards a successful meeting was held. TIIE POPULAR CoNcEras.—The popular penny concert was held as usual in the Bridgewater rooms on Saturday evening, when there was again a large audience. The singing of Mr. Fred. Fieldhouse, of Warrington, was very effective, and secured for him hearty applause. Mr. Robert, also of, Warrington, played a couple of violin solos. Mr. Brown delivered an address, the rest of the programme being filled in by Lyinm friends. Mr. and Mrs. Dodds each gave a reading, and the Misses Thorp and Brown sang. SKATING MATCH.—At a skating. match which took place at Wispeach, Cambridgeshire, on Monday, the champion, James Smart, brother of " Fish " Smart, of Lymm, succeeded in carrying off the first prize, £lO. There were 20 entries, the course being a mile and a half (five turns). Smart's time was smin. 1-ssec. J. Turkey Smart, another brother of the winner, accomplished the distance in smin. 18sec. It may interest our readers to learn that the brothers Smart ' have now held the championship of the world since the year 1878. TEMPERANCE. Msrrisos.—An entertainment under the auspices of the Lymni branch of the above society was given in the Parochial Schools on Tuesday evening, there being a moderate attendance. A service of song was well rendered by the members.—A meeting in connec- tion with the Cheshire Grand Division of the order of the Sons of Temperance was held in the Wesleyan Chapel on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance of the representatives of the order from the surrounding dis- tricts. A number of addresses were delivered, and at the close a collection was taken .in aid of the Lyinin Wesleyan Band of Hope.
The Bank rate of discount is reduced from the 4- to n. per cent.

div.head: MEETING OF DRUIDS AT .WARRINGTON.
div.p: MEETING OF DRUIDS AT .WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening a meeting of members of the Order of Druids in the Warrington district was held in the Masonic Chambers, Sankey-st., at which a reception was given to grand officers of the Order. The visitors present were P.G.M., G. Ingham, G.T., (Manchester), P.G.M., Butterworth (Rochdale), D.C.S. Walker (Worsley and Swinton) senior mem- ber of the Board of Management. The local officers of the Order who were present were D.G.M., 'Thos. Eden, who presided; D.G.M.' James - Simcock , P.D.G.M., Thomas'Roberts.D.C.S. ; P.D.G.M., Samuel Dunbobbin ; P.D.G.M., William Crosskill ; Henry Kent: P,D.G.M.. Henry Lloyd; and P.D.G.M.; Edward Poynton. The CHAIRMAN having introduced the visiting grand officers to the meeting, remarked that there was at pre- sent one great question before the district, and that was the question of forming one common sick fund for the whole of the district.

Bro. S. DuNnonniN next welcomed:the Visiting Officers on behalf of the meeting, and• afterwards spoke strongly in favour of an equalisation of the sick funds of the dis- trict. Thee had two or three lodges in the district that were sufferingfrom want of funds,and on the other hand there were lodges with plenty of money,and equalisation was becoming a necessity. Bro. BUTTERWORTH having spoken, Bro. WALKER followed. He said equalisation was an acknowledged principal in connection with every lodge in the order, and in connection• with every friendly society lodge in the country. If it was wise for indivi- duals to band themselves together to meet certain emer- gencies, he contended that it was wise for lodges to band together to meet emergencies also. This had been done so far as the funeral fund was concerned.

Bro. Memos was the next speaker. He mentioned that one of the finest institutions in the kingdom, the Amalgamated Society for Engineers, was an equalised one, and that the National Sick and Burial Society was the same. There was not the slightest doubt that equa- lisation of the districts would be followed by the equali- sation of the order generally. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN invited questions and none being asked, he proceeded to make some remarks. He hoped every member would act for once as a delegate in bringing about discussion on this subject in his lodge. _ . . .

Brother ROBERTS next spoke in favour O f equalisation, and mentioned that as district corresponding secretary he had obtained statistics from about 22 lodges that were equalised. Brother GIBSON asked if the management expenses could not be reduced in case of equalisation. He did not see that sickness would be any less, and he did not see that the funds would largely increase. Bro: HIGHAM replied that the management expenses had been reduced by • equalisation. Sickness would not be less,,but there would be greater justice and generosity (Applause.) Bro. JAMES MCCOLLOM, P.A., and Bro. Gibson having made some further observations, which elicted remarks frcm Bros. Walker and Roberts.
Bro. CROSKILL proposed a vote of thanks to the grand officers for their addrecses.
Bro. KENT seconded, and Bro. PATTON supported the nation which was carried with acclamation.
A vote of 'thanks to the Chairman concluded the pro- zeedings.
WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL GIFURCH, WARRINGTON. ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

The annual tea meeting in connection with Wycliffe Church was held in Wycliffe Hall, on Thursday evening. The tea was one of the most successful held at Wycliffe, there being present about 500 persons. The tables were presided over by the following ladies :—Mrs. Yonge, Mrs. Armit- age, Mrs. A. Lee, Mx. W. Wallington, Mrs. Garland, Mrs. Podmore, Mrs. Beswick, Mrs. G. Wallington, Mrs. Hawthorn, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Lev,ge, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Corney, Mrs. Wylie, Mrs Birch, Mrs. Parry, Mrs. F. Womersley and Mrs. Rathbone ; Misses Cargill, Beswick, Weir, Blease and Farrer. The Committee which made the arrangements for the tea and subsequent gathering was composed of the following ;—Messrs. Podmore. Beswick, Wylie, Haynes, G. Wallington, T. Hawthorn, Mrs. Wylie, ' and Miss Legge. • After tea a crowded meeting was held, presided over by the Rev. John Yonge. There were also pre- sent—the Rev. E. Moore, Rev. J. Davies, and the following deacons :—Messrs. Z. Armitage, J.P., J. S. Garland, W. Beswick, .G. Wallington; R. Roberts, Podmore, Hawthorn, and Leo. The Ciimnics.sr, in a • few opening remarks, ex- pressed the pleasure they felt at seeing so large a gathering of people in Wycliffe Hall that night. .They had had tea parties there in the past, but he did not rememner ever to have seen so large a meet- ing as they had with them that night. He was afraid that their friends who had . in hand the res- ponsible and onerous duty of providing for the physical wants of their guests, had not in their possession at the fortunate moment a sufficient amount. of faith to enable them to foresee accu- rately how many friends would respond to the invi- tation to come to that meeting, and therefore he had just heard that some of their friends did not get altogether as much tea as they could possibly have enjoyed. They would, however, he trusted, forgive any little defect that they might have found in the commissiariat, and if they came again,and he hoped they would, he had no doubt that they should learn by experience, and have faith to be- lieve that when they issued an invitation for their annual tea they would have a very large gathering to respond to it. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad indeed that they had had such a house-warming. He thought it might be taken as.a very outward and manifest sign that, whatever some of the croackers might have predicted,Wycliffe was not dead yet. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was also verY glad to know,because lie had been speaking to some of them, that they had a number of old • Wycliffe people there that night who had not been. to see_ them of late. All he could say was that they'were glad to see them, and that they elionld be gladder still to see them on Sundays. (Hear, hear.) They should i he exceedingly pleased if some of their friends who, for various reasons, had not been with them lately, should find their way back to the old place. They would give them a hearty welcome, and he thought the friends might use their Sundays in a less profitable way than by attending the ser- vices in Wycliffe Church. (Applause.) He was sure they were very much indebted to their friends who had been given them some lantern illustrations. He was very glad they possessed so admirable a lantern. They had been using it of late in lantern lectures which were but the beginning of a series of such kind of things in the days to come. (Applause.) His own belief was that there was a future for lan-

ijiarlesLyddon was charged on remand at Faversham, on Thursday, with causing his stepbrother's death.— William Bedster said deceased looked very ill the night before his death, but did not appear to have been drink- lug.—Mr. Mowell said he had decided not to call Mrs. Lyddon, and the prosecution closed.—Mr. Mercer said he should not oppose a committal, as it would serve no useful end in view of the verdict of the coroner's jury: Prisoner was committed for trial.

The Press Association says the cause of the death of the Duke of Bedford is now fully and completely estab- lished by the certificate of the registrar of deaths for the distriet of Belgravia. The Duke died on the 14th inst., but the death was not registeted'until the 19th inst, the certificate from Mr. J. Troutbeck, coroner for West- minster, stating that an inquest was held on the 15th January, and the cause of the death was a "Bullet wound in the heart. Verdict of suicide during tempor- ary insanity during pneumonia."

Wallington; instru- mental performances by a string band composed of the following ;—Mr. R. ii. Griffiths; and recitations by Mr. Greener. Although, owing to the length of the programme, encores were not encouraged, both Mr. Griffiths and Mr. Greener were recalled, the former for a song and the latter for a recitation. All the other performances were also, judging by the hearty applause, highly appreciated by the audience.

At the conclusion' the CHAIRMAN asked the audience to acknowledge the services of those who got up the meeting and provided for them a plea- sant programme, and this was done by loud acclam- ation. The successful gathering was brought to a close by the singing of the Doxology.

DEATH OF A SIGNALMAN.

George Parker, the signalmen who was dreadfully in- jured on Tuesday on the railway at Altofts, near Leeds, died at Leeds Infirmary yesterday morning. His com- panion, an engine driver, named Samuel Bailey, was killed on the spot. Both belonged to Northampton. -

div.head: NORTHAMPTONSHIRE MURDER.
div.p: THE NORTHAMPTONSHIRE MURDER.

No clue has been found up to ten o'clock yesterday morning to the murderers of the old man Dickens, whose body was found concealed in a ditch at Rushden, Nor- thamptonshife. It is presumed that he was attacked by poachers. It is supposed the poachers were disturbed by deceased and that they attacked him with his tools, and finally shot him. His money was not touched.

div.head: IRISH LEADERSHIP.
div.p: THE IRISH LEADERSHIP.

Mr. Justin M'Carthy has been in communication with his supporters in Dublin and has, it is understood, requested that the action be postponed in founding the new Anti-Parnaite organisation pending the result of the negotiations for a settlement proceeding at Boulogne. Yesterday Mr. M'Carthy went to Boulogne with the object of again conferring with Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon.

div.head: SCOTCH STRIKE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH STRIKE.

It is reported at the head office of the North British that the guards and signalmen in Dunfermline, Hawick, and other districts are resuming work. At a meeting of the men on strike at Edinburgh yesterday afternoon Mr. Thomson, who presided, referred to the rumours of a settlement, but said there could be no settlement until the companies granted the first demand of the ten-hours day.

div.head: THREE HUNDRED ARRESTS IN PARIS.
div.p: THREE HUNDRED ARRESTS IN PARIS.
PAtus, FRIDAY AFFERNOON.—A serious disturbance took place this afternoon on the piace De L'Opera. The police made three hundred arrests including ten armed anarchists.
DEATH OF THE HEIR TO THE BELGIAN THRONE. EXCITEMENT IN BRUSSELS.

A telegram from Brussels, yesterday morning, states that Prince Baudouin, of Flanders, nephew of King Leopold, and heir to the cram of Belgium, died at three o'clock on Friday morning from bronchitis. The publi- cation of the news there has' caused- an almost unpre- cedented sensation, as the public did not even know that his Royal Highness was ill. Prince Baudouin was iu his 22nd year, having been born June 3, 1869. The brother of the deceased, Prince Albert, now becomes heir to the throne. He is 17 years of age. The sad news has been kept from the Princess Hemrietta, the deceased Prince's sister, who is only now recovering from a severe attack of inflammation of the lungs. King Leopold has received a message from Queen Victoria, expressing. her sympathy with him and his consort in the loss they have sustained. A similar telegram has been received from the Prince of Wales. All the flags in the city are at half-mast. BRUSSELS, FRIDAY AITERWOON.—The latest and most probable cause of Prince Baudouin death is that it was due to a complication of small-pox, bronchitis, and haematuria.

div.head: YESTE RDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: YESTE RDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at half-past four. Two Select Com- mittees were appointed to eontinue the inquiry into the property of metropolitan hospitals, and to consider the Bishop of Peterborough's Children's Life Insurance Bill.' The House adjourned at 25 minutes to 5. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock.

DISESTABLISHMENT.—Mr. P. MORGAN gave notice that he should in four weeks time call attention to the ques- tion of the disestablishment of the Welsh Church, and move a resolution thereon. THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIK R.—Mr. WATT asked" the President of the Board of Trade whether his attention had been called to a recent decision that "the Act of 1854, compelling railway companies, whether it paid them or not, within reasonable limits to afford facilities for the conveyance of all classes of traffic."—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH said his attention had been called to a news- paper reportof the decision referred to. Parliament had not given the Board of Trade any statutory authority to interefere in the manner suggested by. the hon.-member. Such a question was one to be decided, as was done in the case referred to, by a proper legal tribunal, at the in- stance of those who were interested.

THE HOME SECRETARY AND THE DUCAL SIIICIDE.-34r. COBB asked the Home Secretary concerning :the death of the late Duke of Bedford whether it was the custom to give notice to the police of the holding of a coroner's inquiry, and if such notice was given in this cise.—Mr. Morton had also placed a question on the paper regarding the same subject.—Mr. MATTHEWS said he would answer both questions at the same the. He was informed by the coroner that notice was given to the police, and that an inspector of police was present. It was customary, though not obligatory, for the coroner to post Up in his office a list of inquests to be held. The coroner gave no ordersto omit this from the bill, and as a matter of fact it was included. No departure from the usual practice was made in this case. This was an open inquiry in a public court, and anyone might have attended. The coroner knew no reason whylbe public and reporters were not present. As the coroner did not conduct the' inquiry in private the question as to the legal rights did not arise.

CHANNING called at- tention to the excessive hours of labour, and moved that the Board of Trade should Obtain powers by legislation to issue orders, where necessary, directing Railway .COMpaniesto .limit the hours of wor.k.---Mr. Witr..sox (Durham), seconded the motion.—Mr. HOWARTH, as a ministerialist; supported the general tepiour of Mr. Chan.; ring's speech and condemned the disinclination of the Scotch Companies to consult with Trades Union represen- tatives. (Opposition cheers.)—Mr. BecKANA.N referring to the Scotch strike, and to the reasonable attitude ag- sumed by the men undertaking to be bound by the award of Lord Aberdeen, was strongly of opinion that a powerful case had been made out for direct interfe- rence on the part of the Board of Trade or some other Government department. Alunnoen contended that where long hours or overtime was worked by railway servants, it was generally owing to circumstances over 'which the directors had DO control. He thought it would be much better if railway directors and their ser- vants were allowed to settle their differences amongst themselves.—Dr. CRAWFORD condemned the excessive hours railway servants were compelled to work as dan- gerous to the public.

PRESCOT UNION, APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICERS. The Guardians are prepared to receive applications from married persons for the offices of Relieving Officer for the Widnes and Ditton Districts. The Widnes District comprises the townships of Bold and Crouton and a portion of the township of Widnes. The Ditton District con- sists of the remaining portion of the township of Widnes and the townships of Ditton, Hale, Hal,-wood, Speke, Little Wootton, and Much Wootton. The salary of each Officer will commence at £lOO per annum, The persons appointed must reside within their respective districts, and devote the whole of their time to the duties of their .office. Applications stat- ing age, and present occupation with copies of recent testi- monials (Which will not be returned) to be sent to me not later than 10 a.m. on Monday, the 26th January. Bond re- quired through a Guarantee Society for the sum of £l5O for each District. Theappointments will be made subject to the approval of the Local Government Board. Canvassing the Guardians will be a disquatitreation, S. H. HARTLEY, linion Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 15th Jan., 1891.
